LISINOPRIL.clue: ACE inhibitor used for hypertension, diabetic kidney disease, and heart failure; a dry cough is common
LISINOPRIL.rationale: Lisinopril can cause cough, hyperkalemia, and angioedema, and it is teratogenic. A small rise in creatinine can be acceptable; stop it for severe kidney decline or pregnancy.

LOSARTAN.clue: Angiotensin-receptor blocker used when an ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable; still avoided in pregnancy
LOSARTAN.rationale: Losartan does not cause cough as often as an ACE inhibitor, but angioedema can still occur and hyperkalemia is a risk. Do not combine it with an ACE inhibitor.

AMLODIPINE.clue: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker for hypertension; ankle swelling is a common effect
AMLODIPINE.rationale: Amlodipine is a first-line option for many adults, including older adults with isolated systolic hypertension. The edema is from vasodilation and does not by itself mean heart failure; it may be used in reduced ejection fraction, unlike diltiazem or verapamil.

THIAZIDE.clue: First-line diuretic class for hypertension that can lower potassium and raise uric acid and calcium
THIAZIDE.rationale: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics are initial choices for many patients with hypertension. Watch for hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and gout; they raise serum calcium, which distinguishes them from loop diuretics.

METOPROLOL.clue: Beta blocker proven in heart failure only as the succinate salt; do not stop it suddenly
METOPROLOL.rationale: Metoprolol succinate, carvedilol, and bisoprolol are the evidence-based beta blockers for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Abrupt withdrawal can provoke tachycardia or ischemia, and beta blockers can mask hypoglycemia.

CARVEDILOL.clue: Nonselective beta blocker with alpha blockade, taken with food, and proven in systolic heart failure
CARVEDILOL.rationale: Carvedilol lowers blood pressure and heart rate and is one of three beta blockers with outcome data in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Avoid it in asthma and in decompensated, volume-overloaded failure.

BISOPROLOL.clue: Cardioselective beta blocker with outcome data in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
BISOPROLOL.rationale: Bisoprolol is grouped with carvedilol and metoprolol succinate as disease-modifying therapy for HFrEF. Atenolol does not have that role; start low and titrate as blood pressure and perfusion allow.

ATENOLOL.clue: Beta blocker that is not an evidence-based drug for systolic heart failure and is not preferred in pregnancy
ATENOLOL.rationale: Atenolol is sometimes used for rate or blood-pressure control, but it is not disease-modifying therapy for HFrEF. It is renally cleared and has been linked to fetal growth restriction when used in pregnancy.

FUROSEMIDE.clue: Loop diuretic used for fluid overload in heart failure; it wastes potassium and magnesium
FUROSEMIDE.rationale: Furosemide relieves congestion but does not improve survival by itself. Monitor weight, electrolytes, and kidney function; ototoxicity is more likely with high or rapid intravenous doses.

CLONIDINE.clue: Central alpha agonist for blood pressure that can cause rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly
CLONIDINE.rationale: Clonidine is not first-line for hypertension. Sedation and dry mouth are common; taper it, because sudden withdrawal can produce a dangerous rise in blood pressure.

NIFEDIPINE.clue: Calcium-channel blocker used for hypertension in pregnancy; the immediate-release form can drop pressure too fast
NIFEDIPINE.rationale: Extended-release nifedipine is an option for chronic hypertension in pregnancy and is also used for tocolysis. Immediate-release nifedipine is not appropriate long-term therapy because of abrupt hypotension.

LABETALOL.clue: Combined alpha and beta blocker often chosen for severe hypertension in pregnancy
LABETALOL.rationale: Labetalol is a standard treatment for severe-range blood pressure in pregnancy, generally 160 systolic or 110 diastolic or higher. Avoid it in asthma and in heart block.

METHYLDOPA.clue: Older antihypertensive still used in pregnancy; it can cause a positive Coombs test and hepatitis
METHYLDOPA.rationale: Methyldopa has long safety data in pregnancy but often causes sedation. Stop it if liver enzymes rise; a positive Coombs test can interfere with antibody screening.

EPLERENONE.clue: Aldosterone antagonist used in systolic heart failure that does not cause breast enlargement
EPLERENONE.rationale: Eplerenone, like spironolactone, is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist that improves outcomes in HFrEF. The main risk is hyperkalemia, especially with an ACE inhibitor and reduced kidney function; it lacks spironolactone's antiandrogen effects.

SACUBITRIL.clue: Neprilysin inhibitor combined with valsartan for systolic heart failure; allow a washout after an ACE inhibitor
SACUBITRIL.rationale: Sacubitril-valsartan replaces an ACE inhibitor or ARB in eligible patients with HFrEF. Switching from an ACE inhibitor requires about a 36-hour gap because of angioedema risk; it is teratogenic and can cause hypotension and hyperkalemia.

ISOSORBIDE.clue: Long-acting nitrate paired with hydralazine in selected patients with systolic heart failure
ISOSORBIDE.rationale: Hydralazine plus a nitrate is added for some self-identified Black patients who remain symptomatic on guideline therapy, and for patients who cannot take an ACE inhibitor, ARB, or ARNI. Never combine a nitrate with a PDE5 inhibitor.

IVABRADINE.clue: Heart-rate drug added in sinus rhythm when the pulse stays high despite a beta blocker
IVABRADINE.rationale: Ivabradine reduces hospitalizations in selected patients with HFrEF who are in sinus rhythm on a maximized beta blocker. It is not used for rate control of atrial fibrillation and can cause visual brightness.

AMIODARONE.clue: Rhythm drug with lung, thyroid, liver, and skin toxicity and a very long half-life
AMIODARONE.rationale: Amiodarone interacts with warfarin and digoxin and prolongs the QT interval. Check thyroid and liver tests and watch for cough or dyspnea from pulmonary toxicity; photosensitivity and blue-gray skin can occur.

WARFARIN.clue: Oral anticoagulant monitored with INR and reversed with vitamin K; required for mechanical valves
WARFARIN.rationale: Warfarin is teratogenic and has many drug and diet interactions, so vitamin K intake should stay consistent. Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred for most nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, but not for mechanical valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.

APIXABAN.clue: Direct oral anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation and clots; dose is reduced only when specific criteria are met
APIXABAN.rationale: Apixaban does not need routine INR checks. Avoid it with a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis; dose reduction depends on age, weight, and kidney function together, not on one factor alone.

DABIGATRAN.clue: Direct thrombin inhibitor that can cause dyspepsia; a specific antibody reverses it
DABIGATRAN.rationale: Dabigatran is an option for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and for venous thromboembolism. Kidney function limits its use; idarucizumab is the reversal agent for serious bleeding.

CLOPIDOGREL.clue: P2Y12 antiplatelet used after stenting; some proton-pump inhibitors reduce its activation
CLOPIDOGREL.rationale: Clopidogrel is a prodrug. Omeprazole can reduce its effect through CYP2C19, so a different acid reducer is preferred if one is required; bleeding is the main risk, and it is part of dual therapy after many coronary stents.

ASPIRIN.clue: Antiplatelet used for secondary prevention of vascular disease; avoid it in children with a viral illness
ASPIRIN.rationale: Aspirin is standard after atherosclerotic events unless bleeding risk forbids it. Primary prevention is selective, not automatic; in children, aspirin during influenza or varicella is linked to Reye syndrome; Kawasaki disease is a deliberate exception.

SIMVASTATIN.clue: Statin that is taken in the evening and interacts with grapefruit and many CYP3A4 drugs
SIMVASTATIN.rationale: Simvastatin lowers LDL cholesterol. Myalgia is common and true rhabdomyolysis is rare; high doses and interacting drugs raise muscle toxicity; it is contraindicated in pregnancy.

PRAVASTATIN.clue: Statin with fewer cytochrome interactions, chosen when drug interactions limit other agents
PRAVASTATIN.rationale: Pravastatin lowers LDL cholesterol and is less dependent on CYP3A4 than simvastatin. Muscle symptoms and rare liver injury still require counseling; intensity is matched to cardiovascular risk rather than to one fixed dose for everyone.

FENOFIBRATE.clue: Fibrate used for very high triglycerides to lower pancreatitis risk, not as routine add-on prevention
FENOFIBRATE.rationale: Fenofibrate is safer than gemfibrozil if a statin must be combined with a fibrate, but the combination still needs caution. It can cause gallstones and myalgia; lifestyle measures remain first-line for moderate triglyceride elevations.

NIACIN.clue: Older lipid drug that causes flushing and is no longer routine add-on therapy with a statin
NIACIN.rationale: Niacin can worsen glucose and inflame the liver, and outcome trials did not support adding it to a statin for most patients. If it is used, flushing is reduced by taking it with food and sometimes with aspirin if aspirin is otherwise appropriate.

STATIN.clue: Drug class that lowers LDL cholesterol and is the foundation of atherosclerotic risk reduction
STATIN.rationale: Statin intensity follows overall cardiovascular risk, diabetes, and very high LDL cholesterol rather than a single age cutoff. Counsel about muscle pain, rare rhabdomyolysis, and avoidance in pregnancy; check baseline liver enzymes and recheck if symptoms occur.

GRAPEFRUIT.clue: Fruit that raises levels of simvastatin and several calcium-channel blockers through CYP3A4
GRAPEFRUIT.rationale: Grapefruit juice can increase myopathy risk with simvastatin, lovastatin, and atorvastatin. Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are less affected; patients on interacting drugs should keep intake consistent or avoid it.

MYALGIA.clue: Muscle aching that can occur on a statin and must be distinguished from rare muscle breakdown
MYALGIA.rationale: Statin-associated myalgia is usually bilateral and proximal. Dark urine, weakness, or a marked creatine kinase rise suggests rhabdomyolysis and the drug should be stopped; many people tolerate a lower dose or a different statin later.

TROPONIN.clue: Blood marker most specific for myocardial injury; a rising pattern matters more than one value
TROPONIN.rationale: Troponin can be elevated in myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, and kidney disease as well as acute coronary syndrome. Interpret it with the electrocardiogram and the story, not as a standalone diagnosis.

ANGINA.clue: Exertional pressure from myocardial ischemia that is relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
ANGINA.rationale: Typical angina is substernal, provoked by exertion, and relieved by rest. Women, older adults, and people with diabetes more often present with dyspnea, fatigue, or epigastric distress; unstable symptoms need same-day evaluation.

ISCHEMIA.clue: Inadequate blood supply to tissue; in the gut it causes pain out of proportion to the exam
ISCHEMIA.rationale: Mesenteric ischemia is a vascular emergency, especially in atrial fibrillation or severe atherosclerosis. Cardiac ischemia may be silent; either pattern needs urgent evaluation rather than reassurance from a soft abdomen or a normal early exam alone.

DYSPNEA.clue: Shortness of breath that can be the dominant symptom of heart failure, clot, anemia, or ischemia
DYSPNEA.rationale: Sudden dyspnea suggests pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, or flash pulmonary edema. Exertional dyspnea with orthopnea and edema suggests heart failure; in pregnancy, a sudden increase needs evaluation for embolism, anemia, or cardiomyopathy.

ORTHOPNEA.clue: Breathlessness when lying flat, a classic symptom of elevated left-sided filling pressure
ORTHOPNEA.rationale: Patients with orthopnea sleep on extra pillows or sit up. It points to pulmonary congestion; ask about it whenever edema, weight gain, or a new cough appears.

EDEMA.clue: Swelling that may reflect heart failure, a calcium-channel blocker, clot, kidney disease, or low albumin
EDEMA.rationale: Unilateral leg edema suggests deep-vein thrombosis or local injury more than heart failure. Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers cause dependent edema that is not a reason to diagnose heart failure by itself; pitting edema plus orthopnea needs a volume and heart evaluation.

SYNCOPE.clue: Transient loss of consciousness; exertional episodes raise concern for outflow obstruction or arrhythmia
SYNCOPE.rationale: Syncope during exercise, with chest pain, or with a family history of sudden death is cardiac until proven otherwise. Vasovagal syncope usually has a prodrome; obtain an electrocardiogram and review medicines that prolong the QT interval or drop blood pressure.

PALPITATION.clue: Awareness of the heartbeat that may be benign or may signal atrial fibrillation or a dangerous rhythm
PALPITATION.rationale: Ask about sudden onset, duration, syncope, and stimulant or thyroid disease. An electrocardiogram is the first test; irregularly irregular rhythm suggests atrial fibrillation and a stroke-risk decision, not just reassurance.

MURMUR.clue: Sound of turbulent flow; radiation and timing help separate valve lesions from innocent flow
MURMUR.rationale: A systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids suggests aortic stenosis. A holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla suggests mitral regurgitation; diastolic murmurs are pathologic and need echocardiography.

STENOSIS.clue: Narrowing of a valve; the aortic form causes a harsh systolic murmur and can present with chest pain, fainting, or breathlessness
STENOSIS.rationale: Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis is a reason for valve replacement referral, and vasodilation can cause hypotension. Pulsus parvus et tardus is the small, delayed carotid upstroke; rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with a diastolic rumble and an opening snap.

AORTIC.clue: Valve whose stenosis radiates to the neck and whose regurgitation causes a blowing diastolic murmur
AORTIC.rationale: Aortic stenosis is a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur. Aortic regurgitation is a diastolic decrescendo murmur with a wide pulse pressure; both need echocardiography when the exam or symptoms suggest significant disease.

MITRAL.clue: Valve whose regurgitation is holosystolic at the apex and whose prolapse causes a mid-systolic click
MITRAL.rationale: Mitral regurgitation often radiates toward the axilla. Mitral stenosis is usually rheumatic and becomes symptomatic when pregnancy or atrial fibrillation increases demand; prolapse is often benign but needs evaluation if there is significant regurgitation.

CLICK.clue: Mid-systolic sound of mitral valve prolapse, often followed by a late systolic murmur
CLICK.rationale: The click and murmur of mitral valve prolapse move earlier when venous return falls, such as with standing or the Valsalva maneuver. Most people need only surveillance unless regurgitation or symptoms are significant.

RUMBLE.clue: Low diastolic murmur of mitral stenosis, often with an opening snap
RUMBLE.rationale: Mitral stenosis is a consequence of rheumatic heart disease. Pregnancy can precipitate pulmonary edema because cardiac output and heart rate rise; refer for echocardiography rather than labeling the sound innocent.

VALSALVA.clue: Bearing-down maneuver that makes the murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy louder
VALSALVA.rationale: Reduced preload intensifies hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mitral-valve prolapse murmurs and softens most flow murmurs. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a cause of exertional syncope and sudden death in athletes and needs activity restriction until evaluated.

GALLOP.clue: Extra heart sound; a third heart sound in an adult suggests volume overload or systolic failure
GALLOP.rationale: An S3 gallop is common and often normal in children and pregnancy, but in an older adult it points to heart failure. An S4 suggests a stiff ventricle; confirm with the history, exam, and natriuretic peptide or imaging as needed.

BRUIT.clue: Vascular sound of turbulent flow, heard over a narrowed carotid or renal artery or a goiter
BRUIT.rationale: A carotid bruit raises the possibility of stenosis and needs correlation with symptoms and imaging when stroke risk is a concern. Do not massage both carotids; an abdominal bruit with resistant hypertension suggests renal-artery stenosis.

JUGULAR.clue: Neck vein whose elevation reflects high right-sided filling pressure
JUGULAR.rationale: Jugular venous distension supports heart failure, fluid overload, or constriction when the patient is positioned correctly. It is more specific for elevated venous pressure than ankle swelling alone.

BNP.clue: Natriuretic peptide that rises when the ventricle is stretched; obesity can lower the value
BNP.rationale: BNP or NT-proBNP helps when the cause of dyspnea is uncertain. Levels also rise with kidney failure, pulmonary embolism, and atrial fibrillation; a normal value makes acute heart failure less likely but does not replace clinical judgment.

FRACTION.clue: Percent of ventricular volume expelled each beat; forty percent or less marks systolic heart failure
FRACTION.rationale: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is generally a fraction of 40 percent or less. Guideline therapy includes an ARNI or ACE inhibitor or ARB, an evidence-based beta blocker, a mineralocorticoid antagonist, an SGLT2 inhibitor, and a diuretic if congested.

IRREGULAR.clue: Rhythm without a pattern, the usual pulse of atrial fibrillation
IRREGULAR.rationale: Atrial fibrillation needs a rate strategy and a stroke-prevention decision based on a risk score, not on whether sinus rhythm returns. Anticoagulation is long-term for most patients with elevated risk; a direct oral anticoagulant is preferred when there is no mechanical valve or significant mitral stenosis.

VERAPAMIL.clue: Non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker that treats rate and cluster-headache prevention but worsens systolic failure
VERAPAMIL.rationale: Verapamil can cause constipation and bradycardia and should not be stacked casually with a beta blocker. It is a prophylactic option for cluster headache; it is contraindicated in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

TIA.clue: Transient focal neurologic deficit that is a warning stroke and needs same-day evaluation
TIA.rationale: A TIA is not a minor event to schedule for later in the week. Short-term stroke risk is high; some high-risk patients receive a short course of dual antiplatelet therapy after bleeding has been excluded; carotid imaging and rhythm evaluation are part of the workup.

STROKE.clue: Sudden focal brain deficit; the last time the person was well determines eligibility for reperfusion
STROKE.rationale: Use a face-arm-speech check and obtain imaging promptly to distinguish ischemia from bleeding. Do not give aspirin until hemorrhage is excluded if thrombolysis is being considered; time windows depend on imaging and the current protocol, so activate emergency care rather than calculating eligibility in the clinic.

ALTEPLASE.clue: Thrombolytic considered for eligible ischemic stroke; bleeding risk is the major harm
ALTEPLASE.rationale: Alteplase is time-sensitive and contraindicated with active bleeding, recent major surgery, or hemorrhage on imaging. Primary care follow-up focuses on cause, blood pressure, statin and antiplatelet therapy, and risk-factor control after the acute decision is made.

APHASIA.clue: Language impairment from a dominant-hemisphere lesion, distinct from dysarthria
APHASIA.rationale: Aphasia can be fluent or nonfluent and is a focal sign of stroke or mass until proven otherwise. Dysarthria is a motor speech problem with intact language; either one with sudden onset is an emergency.

HEMIPARESIS.clue: Weakness of one side of the body, a classic sign of stroke or a structural brain lesion
HEMIPARESIS.rationale: Sudden hemiparesis needs emergency imaging and a last-known-well time. Gradual hemiparesis suggests mass, multiple sclerosis, or Todd paralysis after a seizure; forehead-sparing facial weakness points to a central lesion rather than Bell palsy.

CAROTID.clue: Artery whose stenosis can cause retinal or hemispheric ischemic symptoms
CAROTID.rationale: Amaurosis fugax and a bruit are clues. Symptomatic high-grade stenosis may need revascularization plus intensive medical therapy; asymptomatic stenosis is managed with risk-factor treatment and selective referral.

FAST.clue: Face, arm, and speech mnemonic that prompts emergency care for suspected stroke
FAST.rationale: Any sudden facial droop, arm weakness, or speech change is treated as stroke until imaging says otherwise. Note the last time the person was known to be well; do not give food or drink until swallowing is assessed.

DVT.clue: Clot in a deep leg vein; unilateral swelling and risk factors matter more than calf tenderness
DVT.rationale: Homans sign is unreliable. Use a pretest score and, when probability is low, a D-dimer; otherwise obtain duplex ultrasound; treat confirmed clots with anticoagulation unless a contraindication forces another plan; cancer, estrogen, immobility, and prior clot raise risk.

EMBOLISM.clue: Traveling clot; in the lung it causes sudden dyspnea, chest pain, and sometimes hemoptysis
EMBOLISM.rationale: Pulmonary embolism can present with a normal leg exam. Unstable patients need emergency care, not an outpatient D-dimer; anticoagulation treats both the lung clot and the usual venous source; pregnancy and the postpartum period are high-risk times.

THROMBOSIS.clue: Pathologic clot in a vein or artery; Virchow described stasis, vessel injury, and hypercoagulability
THROMBOSIS.rationale: Estrogen therapy, cancer, surgery, and inherited thrombophilia promote venous clots. Arterial thrombosis is more often platelet-driven, which is why antiplatelet drugs are used after atherosclerotic events; anticoagulants treat venous disease.

WELLS.clue: Pretest score that decides whether a D-dimer can safely exclude a venous clot
WELLS.rationale: A D-dimer is useful only when clinical probability is low. A positive D-dimer is not a diagnosis; high probability goes straight to definitive imaging; the score includes signs, alternative diagnoses, heart rate, immobility, and prior clot.

DDIMER.clue: Fibrin fragment used to rule out clot when pretest probability is low; a positive result is nonspecific
DDIMER.rationale: D-dimer rises with age, pregnancy, infection, and cancer. Do not use it to confirm deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism; a negative result in a low-probability patient makes acute clot unlikely.

HOMANS.clue: Calf-pain sign that is too unreliable to diagnose or exclude a deep-vein thrombosis
HOMANS.rationale: A positive or negative Homans sign should not change the plan. Use a clinical probability score, D-dimer when appropriate, and duplex ultrasound; teaching this limitation prevents false reassurance.

VIRCHOW.clue: Name attached to the triad of stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability
VIRCHOW.rationale: Virchow's triad explains why surgery, travel, cancer, trauma, and estrogen raise clot risk. Prevention after high-risk procedures uses early mobility and, when indicated, pharmacologic prophylaxis.

INR.clue: Clotting test used to monitor warfarin, not the direct oral anticoagulants
INR.rationale: The usual INR goal for most warfarin indications is the standard therapeutic range, with a higher goal for some mechanical valves. Illness, antibiotics, and diet change the value; serious bleeding needs vitamin K and a clotting-factor strategy, not warfarin alone.

VITAMINK.clue: Cofactor warfarin antagonizes; newborns receive an injection to prevent hemorrhagic disease
VITAMINK.rationale: Consistent dietary vitamin K matters more than avoidance for people on warfarin. Phytonadione reverses warfarin and is also the newborn injection that prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding; oral newborn regimens are less reliable than the injection.

PROTAMINE.clue: Antidote that fully reverses unfractionated heparin and only partly reverses low-molecular-weight heparin
PROTAMINE.rationale: Protamine can cause hypotension and hypersensitivity, especially with prior exposure to NPH insulin or fish allergy. It is not the reversal agent for warfarin or for the direct oral anticoagulants.

HEPARIN.clue: Parenteral anticoagulant monitored with aPTT or anti-Xa; it does not cross the placenta
HEPARIN.rationale: Unfractionated heparin is preferred when rapid reversal may be needed. Long-term use can cause osteoporosis; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is an immune complication that requires stopping all heparin and using a non-heparin anticoagulant.

ASTHMA.clue: Episodic wheeze and cough with reversible airflow obstruction; an inhaled corticosteroid is the controller foundation
ASTHMA.rationale: Asthma diagnosis is confirmed with spirometry and bronchodilator reversibility when possible. A short-acting bronchodilator relieves symptoms but should not be the only long-term treatment; inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol can serve as the reliever in current stepwise care.

ALBUTEROL.clue: Short-acting bronchodilator that relieves bronchospasm but does not treat airway inflammation
ALBUTEROL.rationale: Albuterol causes tremor and tachycardia. Using it most days means control is poor and an inhaled corticosteroid should be added or intensified; it is a rescue drug, not anti-inflammatory therapy.

BUDESONIDE.clue: Inhaled corticosteroid with the most pregnancy safety data among medicines in its class
BUDESONIDE.rationale: Budesonide reduces airway inflammation and is a controller, not a reliever by itself. Rinse the mouth and use a spacer to lower the risk of oral thrush; it is the preferred inhaled corticosteroid when one is needed in pregnancy.

FORMOTEROL.clue: Fast-onset long-acting bronchodilator that, combined with an inhaled corticosteroid, can be the reliever
FORMOTEROL.rationale: Formoterol should not be used alone for asthma. Paired with an inhaled corticosteroid it treats both symptoms and inflammation; long-acting bronchodilator monotherapy in asthma increases serious exacerbation risk.

MONTELUKAST.clue: Leukotriene blocker for asthma and allergic rhinitis that carries a neuropsychiatric warning
MONTELUKAST.rationale: Montelukast is not first-line controller therapy. Counsel about mood change, agitation, sleep disturbance, and suicidal thinking, and stop it if those appear; it is taken in the evening in traditional dosing.

FLUTICASONE.clue: Corticosteroid used inhaled for asthma or nasally as the most effective single drug for allergic rhinitis
FLUTICASONE.rationale: Intranasal fluticasone is aimed away from the septum to limit bleeding. Inhaled use requires mouth rinsing to prevent thrush; benefit for nasal congestion exceeds that of an oral antihistamine alone.

SPACER.clue: Holding chamber that improves inhaled-corticosteroid delivery and reduces medicine left in the mouth
SPACER.rationale: A spacer with a pressurized inhaler increases lung deposition and lowers oral thrush. Children and anyone who cannot coordinate a puff should use one; review technique before stepping up therapy.

SPIROMETRY.clue: Lung-function test that shows obstruction and reversibility and should precede a long-term label of asthma or COPD
SPIROMETRY.rationale: A low FEV1/FVC ratio indicates obstruction. A meaningful bronchodilator response supports asthma; COPD is less reversible; do not rely on symptoms alone when this test is available.

PEAKFLOW.clue: Home expiratory measure compared with a personal best to guide an asthma action plan
PEAKFLOW.rationale: Peak-flow zones are based on the patient's own best value, not a population table alone. Falling readings can warn of a flare before severe distress; technique and effort change the number, so coach both.

WHEEZE.clue: Musical breath sound of narrowed airways; its disappearance in a tiring patient can mean impending failure
WHEEZE.rationale: Wheeze occurs in asthma, COPD, heart failure, and foreign-body aspiration. A silent chest after loud wheeze is a red flag for respiratory failure, not improvement; unilateral wheeze suggests a focal obstruction.

TRIGGER.clue: Exposure such as virus, allergen, smoke, exercise, or aspirin that sets off bronchospasm
TRIGGER.rationale: Identifying triggers guides avoidance and explains poor control. Aspirin or NSAID sensitivity with nasal polyps is Samter triad and those drugs should be avoided; gastroesophageal reflux and workplace exposures are worth asking about.

COPD.clue: Smoking-related obstructive disease treated with bronchodilators, rehabilitation, vaccines, and oxygen when hypoxemia is severe
COPD.rationale: Smoking cessation changes the course of COPD more than any inhaler. Long-acting bronchodilators are central; inhaled corticosteroids are added for frequent exacerbations or higher eosinophils and raise pneumonia risk; do not use chronic oral steroids as maintenance.

TIOTROPIUM.clue: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist that is a foundation bronchodilator for COPD
TIOTROPIUM.rationale: Tiotropium dries secretions and can precipitate urinary retention or worsen narrow-angle glaucoma if the mist reaches the eye. It is also an add-on option in asthma that stays uncontrolled on an inhaled corticosteroid and a long-acting beta agonist.

IPRATROPIUM.clue: Short-acting anticholinergic bronchodilator used in COPD flares and for watery rhinorrhea
IPRATROPIUM.rationale: Ipratropium is often nebulized with albuterol during an exacerbation. It is not a daily controller by itself; nasal ipratropium helps nonallergic rhinorrhea; caution still applies if the drug contacts the eye.

PURSED.clue: Lip-breathing technique that slows expiration and reduces air trapping in obstructive lung disease
PURSED.rationale: Pursed-lip breathing is a low-cost skill for COPD dyspnea. Inhale through the nose and exhale slowly through lips that are nearly closed; pair it with pulmonary rehabilitation and smoking cessation.

OXYGEN.clue: Gas that improves survival in COPD with severe resting hypoxemia and that also aborts cluster headache
OXYGEN.rationale: Long-term continuous oxygen is prescribed for severe resting hypoxemia, not for breathlessness with adequate saturation. In patients who retain carbon dioxide, the target saturation is modest rather than normal; high-flow oxygen is an acute treatment for cluster headache.

SPUTUM.clue: Lower-airway mucus; a change in color, volume, or thickness helps define a COPD exacerbation
SPUTUM.rationale: Purulent sputum plus increased dyspnea and volume supports a bacterial exacerbation in the right host. Bloody sputum needs evaluation for infection, clot, bronchitis, or malignancy; sputum is not required to diagnose uncomplicated acute bronchitis.

EMPHYSEMA.clue: Destruction of alveolar walls that causes air trapping; early or basilar disease suggests alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
EMPHYSEMA.rationale: Emphysema is a COPD phenotype. Smoking cessation is essential; test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency when disease appears young, is basilar, or there is a family history; oxygen and bronchodilators treat the physiology, not the destroyed alveoli.

BRONCHITIS.clue: Airway inflammation; the acute form in healthy adults is usually viral and does not need an antibiotic
BRONCHITIS.rationale: Acute bronchitis causes cough that can last weeks. Colored sputum alone does not prove a bacterial infection; reserve antibiotics for pneumonia or a significant COPD exacerbation; chronic bronchitis is a COPD phenotype defined by a prolonged productive cough.

PNEUMONIA.clue: Lung infection with fever, cough, and an infiltrate; healthy outpatients are often treated with amoxicillin or doxycycline
PNEUMONIA.rationale: Community-acquired pneumonia in adults with comorbidities needs broader coverage than amoxicillin alone. Severity, oxygen saturation, and oral intake decide the site of care; confusion and low blood pressure are danger signs.

LEGIONELLA.clue: Atypical pneumonia organism linked to water aerosols, diarrhea, and low sodium
LEGIONELLA.rationale: Legionella is not seen on a routine Gram stain and does not respond to a beta-lactam alone. A macrolide or a fluoroquinolone is active; hyponatremia and gastrointestinal symptoms are classic clues in a severe pneumonia.

FLU.clue: Abrupt fever, myalgia, and cough; antiviral treatment works best when started early and vaccine is given each season
FLU.rationale: Oseltamivir is most useful within the first two days in outpatients and is still considered for severe or high-risk illness later. The injectable vaccine is used in pregnancy; the live nasal vaccine is not.

OSELTAMIVIR.clue: Neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza that is most effective when started early in the illness
OSELTAMIVIR.rationale: Oseltamivir can cause nausea and neuropsychiatric symptoms, especially in children. Start it as soon as influenza is likely in high-risk patients rather than waiting for every confirmatory test; it is not a substitute for vaccination.

COVID.clue: Coronavirus illness whose vaccine formulation and antiviral eligibility follow the current seasonal guidance
COVID.rationale: Supportive care is enough for many low-risk outpatients. People at high risk of severe disease should be considered for early antiviral therapy under the current criteria; isolate while contagious and do not use antibiotics for uncomplicated viral disease.

SINUSITIS.clue: Facial pain and nasal congestion that are usually viral unless symptoms are prolonged, severe, or double-worsening
SINUSITIS.rationale: Most acute rhinosinusitis resolves without an antibiotic. When bacterial disease is likely, amoxicillin-clavulanate is a typical first choice, not a macrolide; intranasal corticosteroid helps congestion; orbital swelling or severe headache needs urgent care.

RHINITIS.clue: Nasal inflammation that is allergic, viral, or nonallergic; an intranasal corticosteroid is the best single allergic treatment
RHINITIS.rationale: Allergic rhinitis causes itch, sneeze, and clear rhinorrhea and is associated with asthma. Oral second-generation antihistamines help itch and sneeze more than congestion; first-generation antihistamines are poor choices in older adults.

PHARYNGITIS.clue: Sore throat that is usually viral; test for group A strep when Centor features make streptococcus plausible
PHARYNGITIS.rationale: Cough, coryza, and hoarseness point to a virus and do not need a strep test. Penicillin or amoxicillin treats confirmed strep; avoid amoxicillin if infectious mononucleosis is likely, because a rash is common.

CENTOR.clue: Score using fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior neck nodes, and absence of cough to estimate strep throat
CENTOR.rationale: Low Centor scores do not need testing. Higher scores are tested with a rapid antigen test rather than treated blindly in most settings; antibiotics prevent rheumatic fever but do not reliably prevent post-strep glomerulonephritis.

PENICILLIN.clue: First-line drug for group A strep throat and for syphilis at every stage
PENICILLIN.rationale: Penicillin remains the treatment of rheumatic fever prevention after strep pharyngitis and is the only adequate treatment for syphilis in pregnancy. A true immediate allergy needs desensitization for syphilis rather than a switch that may fail.

SCARLET.clue: Sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue that follow streptococcal pharyngitis and are treated like strep throat
SCARLET.rationale: Scarlet fever shows Pastia lines in skin folds and later desquamation. Treatment is penicillin or amoxicillin, the same goal as strep pharyngitis: prevent rheumatic fever and shorten contagiousness; it is not a separate pathogen.

SANDPAPER.clue: Texture of the scarlatiniform rash, a clue that a sore throat is streptococcal
SANDPAPER.rationale: The sandpaper rash of scarlet fever usually spares the area around the mouth and may peel later. Treat the streptococcal infection; a similar rough rash can be seen in other toxin-mediated illnesses, so use the whole picture.

STRAWBERRY.clue: Bright red tongue of scarlet fever and of Kawasaki disease
STRAWBERRY.rationale: In scarlet fever the strawberry tongue accompanies a sandpaper rash and pharyngitis. In Kawasaki disease it accompanies prolonged fever and mucocutaneous signs and is treated with immune globulin plus aspirin, an intentional exception to usual pediatric aspirin avoidance.

PASTIA.clue: Dark lines in skin folds that support scarlet fever
PASTIA.rationale: Pastia lines are accentuated erythema in the antecubital fossae and other creases. They support streptococcal scarlet fever when fever and pharyngitis are present; treatment follows confirmed or highly likely group A strep.

KAWASAKI.clue: Prolonged childhood fever with mucous-membrane changes, rash, and extremity swelling that threatens the coronary arteries
KAWASAKI.rationale: Kawasaki disease is treated promptly with intravenous immune globulin and aspirin to reduce coronary aneurysms. Do not wait out a fever that has lasted many days with conjunctival injection and a polymorphous rash; incomplete cases still need referral.

CORONARY.clue: Arteries that can aneurysm after Kawasaki disease and that cause ischemic chest pain in adults
CORONARY.rationale: Kawasaki follow-up looks for coronary complications. In adults, coronary disease presents with pressure, dyspnea, or atypical symptoms and is prevented with smoking cessation, a statin when indicated, blood pressure control, and antiplatelet therapy after an event.

MONO.clue: Epstein-Barr illness with profound fatigue and splenomegaly; amoxicillin often causes a rash
MONO.rationale: Infectious mononucleosis shows posterior cervical nodes more than the anterior nodes of strep. The heterophile test can be negative early; avoid contact sports until the spleen is no longer enlarged; the amoxicillin rash does not prove a lifelong penicillin allergy.

SPLEEN.clue: Organ that enlarges in mononucleosis and can rupture with contact sports
SPLEEN.rationale: Left-upper-quadrant pain or referred shoulder pain after mono is a rupture until proven otherwise. Also examine the spleen in suspected leukemia or hemolysis; palpation should be gentle.

EBV.clue: Herpesvirus that causes mononucleosis and is linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma and some lymphomas
EBV.rationale: Epstein-Barr virus is spread by saliva. Fatigue can last weeks; splenomegaly is the reason for activity restriction; a negative heterophile test in the first week does not exclude it.

QUINSY.clue: Peritonsillar abscess with trismus, a muffled voice, and deviation of the uvula
QUINSY.rationale: Quinsy is a deep-neck infection, not simple pharyngitis. Drainage plus antibiotics are required, and airway compromise is the danger; refer rather than repeating oral antibiotics alone.

TRISMUS.clue: Lockjaw from a peritonsillar abscess or from tetanus
TRISMUS.rationale: Trismus with a hot-potato voice and uvular deviation means peritonsillar abscess. Trismus with muscle spasms after a wound suggests tetanus and needs immunoglobulin plus vaccine management and airway protection.

UVULA.clue: Midline structure that shifts away from a peritonsillar abscess
UVULA.rationale: Uvular deviation, unilateral swelling, and trismus distinguish peritonsillar abscess from routine tonsillitis. Allergic uvular edema can also threaten the airway and is treated as anaphylaxis when breathing is affected.

CROUP.clue: Barking cough and hoarseness from subglottic swelling; a corticosteroid is given and severe cases need nebulized epinephrine
CROUP.rationale: Croup is usually viral and shows a steeple sign if imaged, which is not required for typical cases. Stridor at rest needs emergency care; do not examine the throat if epiglottitis is the real concern.

STRIDOR.clue: High-pitched inspiratory sound of upper-airway obstruction
STRIDOR.rationale: Stridor is a red flag in croup, foreign-body aspiration, anaphylaxis, and epiglottitis. Agitation can worsen it, so keep the child calm; epiglottitis features drooling and a tripod posture and the throat is not examined in the clinic.

BARKING.rationale: A barking cough with hoarseness and inspiratory stridor is croup until a more dangerous airway lesion is suspected. Give a corticosteroid; nebulized epinephrine is for significant distress and the child is then observed for rebound.

STEEPLE.clue: Radiographic narrowing of the subglottic trachea seen in croup
STEEPLE.rationale: The steeple sign supports croup but is not required to treat a typical barking cough. Epiglottitis instead shows a thumb sign and a toxic, drooling patient; do not send an unstable airway to imaging.

DROOLING.clue: Sign of epiglottitis or of a retropharyngeal or peritonsillar infection; do not force a throat exam
DROOLING.rationale: Drooling, distress, and a tripod posture suggest epiglottitis. Keep the child with a parent and arrange a secure airway; Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine prevents many classic cases, but other bacteria still cause the disease.

TRIPOD.clue: Forward-leaning posture that a child uses to keep a swollen epiglottis from occluding the airway
TRIPOD.rationale: Tripoding with drooling and muffling is an airway emergency. Do not lay the child flat or use a tongue blade; the same posture can appear in severe respiratory distress from other causes.

HEMOPHILUS.clue: Bacterium whose type b form caused epiglottitis and meningitis before routine infant immunization
HEMOPHILUS.rationale: Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine is given in infancy. Unimmunized children remain at risk for epiglottitis and invasive disease; nontypeable strains still cause otitis and sinusitis and are not covered by that vaccine's full story.

PERTUSSIS.clue: Whooping cough prevented by a booster in every pregnancy and treated with a macrolide
PERTUSSIS.rationale: Pertussis has catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages. Infants may apnea without a whoop; early macrolide treatment and postexposure antibiotics for close contacts reduce spread; maternal immunization protects the newborn.

WHOOP.clue: Inspiratory gasp after a paroxysm of coughing, classic for pertussis but often absent in infants
WHOOP.rationale: The whoop follows a coughing fit that can end in vomiting. Infants are the group most likely to stop breathing instead of whooping; a macrolide is used for treatment and for close-contact prevention.

MACROLIDE.clue: Antibiotic class used for pertussis, many atypical pneumonias, and some mycobacterial or skin infections
MACROLIDE.rationale: Macrolides prolong the QT interval and interact with other QT drugs and with some statins. Azithromycin is not preferred for strep throat or for uncomplicated chlamydia; resistance limits macrolide monotherapy for community pneumonia in many communities.

RSV.clue: Virus that causes bronchiolitis in infants; care is supportive, and routine bronchodilators or steroids are not useful
RSV.rationale: Bronchiolitis treatment is hydration, nasal suction, and oxygen if saturation is low. Antibiotics, albuterol, and corticosteroids are not routine; immunization products for infants and for late pregnancy follow the current schedule.

SMOKING.clue: The exposure whose cessation is the most effective disease-modifying step in COPD and a major cardiovascular intervention
SMOKING.rationale: Ask about tobacco at visits and combine counseling with nicotine replacement, varenicline, or bupropion when the person is ready. Smoking multiplies the clot risk of estrogen contraception, especially at older reproductive ages; it is also the dominant risk for lung and many other cancers.

NICOTINE.clue: Replacement therapy that reduces withdrawal and is more effective when a long-acting form is combined with a short-acting form
NICOTINE.rationale: Nicotine patch plus gum or lozenge outperforms either alone for many people. It is safer than continued smoking in most cardiac patients; combine it with behavioral support; varenicline is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for cessation.

VARENICLINE.clue: Partial nicotinic agonist that is the most effective single drug for smoking cessation
VARENICLINE.rationale: Varenicline is started before a quit date and continued as a course. Nausea and vivid dreams are common; current evidence does not support withholding it solely because of a stable psychiatric history, but mood should still be monitored.

TOBACCO.clue: Product to ask about at every preventive visit; advice plus medicine outperforms advice alone
TOBACCO.rationale: Tobacco use disorder is treated with the same seriousness as other chronic disease. Offer cessation at each visit without requiring perfect readiness; secondhand exposure matters for children with asthma and for pregnancy.

PREDNISONE.clue: Oral corticosteroid used as a short burst for an asthma exacerbation and as a bridge, not as casual long-term therapy
PREDNISONE.rationale: A prednisone burst of up to about two weeks often does not need a taper, but chronic use must not be stopped suddenly. Harms include hyperglycemia, mood change, insomnia, infection, bone loss, and adrenal suppression; give the morning dose with food.

STEROID.clue: Anti-inflammatory class given as one systemic dose for croup and inhaled for persistent asthma
STEROID.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids are the controller foundation in asthma. Systemic steroids treat flares and many inflammatory diseases but cause glucose elevation, bone loss, and adrenal suppression when prolonged; taper chronic therapy; they do not replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis.

DIABETES.clue: Chronic hyperglycemia; type 2 care starts with lifestyle and usually metformin if kidney function allows
DIABETES.rationale: Diagnosis uses fasting glucose, a glucose tolerance test, or glycated hemoglobin, confirmed unless the presentation is unequivocal. Screen adults with overweight or additional risk rather than waiting for symptoms; individualize the glucose target.

METFORMIN.clue: First-line oral agent for type 2 diabetes that can deplete vitamin B12 and rarely causes lactic acidosis
METFORMIN.rationale: Metformin is held when kidney function is acutely worse or severely reduced, including around some contrast studies and during serious illness. Gastrointestinal effects are common and improve with food and slow titration; it does not cause hypoglycemia by itself.

SEMAGLUTIDE.clue: GLP-1 receptor agonist that lowers glucose and weight and has cardiovascular benefit; avoid it with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma
SEMAGLUTIDE.rationale: Semaglutide causes nausea and a feeling of fullness and has a warning for gallbladder disease. Do not combine it with a DPP-4 inhibitor; rapid glucose improvement has been linked to temporary worsening of retinopathy; delayed gastric emptying matters around anesthesia.

LIRAGLUTIDE.clue: Daily GLP-1 receptor agonist with cardiovascular outcome data and a thyroid C-cell tumor warning
LIRAGLUTIDE.rationale: Liraglutide is injected daily, unlike weekly agents in the same class. Gastrointestinal effects are the usual reason for stopping; it is contraindicated with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2.

SITAGLIPTIN.clue: DPP-4 inhibitor that is weight neutral and rarely causes hypoglycemia, and that should not be combined with a GLP-1 agonist
SITAGLIPTIN.rationale: Sitagliptin needs a kidney-based dose adjustment, unlike linagliptin. Pancreatitis has been reported; some other DPP-4 inhibitors, not this one, have a heart-failure signal; it does not cause the weight loss seen with GLP-1 agonists.

GLYBURIDE.clue: Sulfonylurea on the Beers list because hypoglycemia can be prolonged, especially in older adults
GLYBURIDE.rationale: Glyburide and its active metabolites accumulate when kidney function falls. Prefer shorter-acting sulfonylureas if that class is required; it is not first-line for type 2 diabetes and is not the preferred medicine for gestational diabetes.

INSULIN.clue: Hormone replacement required in type 1 diabetes and preferred when gestational diabetes needs medication
INSULIN.rationale: Never stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes on a sick day; check glucose and ketones and keep up fluids. Rotate injection sites to prevent lipohypertrophy; hypoglycemia is the limiting adverse effect; insulin is preferred over oral agents when pregnancy diabetes needs a drug.

GLARGINE.clue: Long-acting basal insulin with no pronounced peak; do not mix it in the same syringe
GLARGINE.rationale: Insulin glargine covers background needs and is usually given once daily. Mealtime insulin is added separately when post-meal glucose stays high; do not mix glargine with rapid or regular insulin.

LISPRO.clue: Rapid-acting insulin given when a meal is in front of the person; its main risk is hypoglycemia
LISPRO.rationale: Lispro, aspart, and glulisine cover meals and correction doses. Inject when food is available; the peak is much earlier than NPH or regular insulin; use it as bolus therapy, not as the only basal insulin.

NPH.clue: Intermediate insulin with a peak several hours after injection; it can be mixed with rapid or regular insulin
NPH.rationale: NPH is cloudy and should be rolled, not shaken hard. When mixing, draw the clear rapid or regular insulin before the cloudy NPH; bedtime dosing can cause nocturnal hypoglycemia, so check a middle-of-the-night glucose if mornings are confusing.

GLUCAGON.clue: Rescue hormone for severe hypoglycemia when the person cannot safely swallow
GLUCAGON.rationale: Give glucagon by injection or nasal spray, then turn the person on the side because vomiting is common. Once awake, give carbohydrate; family should know where the kit is; glucagon is also used in beta-blocker overdose.

GLUCOSE.clue: Sugar measured fasting, after meals, and during illness; fifteen grams of fast carbohydrate treats mild hypoglycemia
GLUCOSE.rationale: Recheck glucose about fifteen minutes after treatment and repeat if it is still low, then give a longer-acting snack. Continuous monitors help but fingerstick confirmation is used when symptoms and the reading disagree; urine glucose is obsolete for management.

KETONE.clue: Acidic product of fat breakdown that appears when insulin is lacking, especially on sick days in type 1 diabetes
KETONE.rationale: Moderate or large ketones with high glucose suggest diabetic ketoacidosis and need urgent care. Illness is a reason to check them even if appetite is poor; SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with a near-normal glucose.

DKA.clue: Anion-gap acidosis with ketones, usually in type 1 diabetes; fluids come first and potassium is often depleted
DKA.rationale: Diabetic ketoacidosis presents with nausea, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul breathing. Do not start insulin until potassium is known, because the serum value can be normal while total-body potassium is low; find the trigger, often infection or missed insulin.

HHS.clue: Extremely high glucose with severe dehydration and little ketoacidosis, usually in older adults with type 2 diabetes
HHS.rationale: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state has higher glucose and more profound volume loss than typical ketoacidosis, and ketones are minimal. It still needs emergency fluids and insulin; altered mentation is common.

KUSSMAUL.clue: Deep, rapid breathing that compensates for the metabolic acidosis of ketoacidosis
KUSSMAUL.rationale: Kussmaul respirations blow off carbon dioxide to raise pH. They are a late clue to diabetic ketoacidosis, not a primary lung disease; treat the acidosis and volume loss rather than suppressing the drive to breathe.

POLYURIA.clue: Excess urine from hyperglycemia or from diabetes insipidus; the first has sweet urine and high glucose, the second does not
POLYURIA.rationale: Osmotic polyuria of uncontrolled diabetes comes with polydipsia and polyphagia. Diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine with normal glucose; nocturia is the symptom patients notice first.

POLYDIPSIA.clue: Excessive thirst that accompanies uncontrolled diabetes or diabetes insipidus
POLYDIPSIA.rationale: Polydipsia with polyuria and weight loss is classic new diabetes. Primary polydipsia is driven by water intake and is distinguished by a water-deprivation evaluation, not by a single glucose.

POLYPHAGIA.clue: Increased hunger that, with thirst and excess urine, suggests insulin deficiency
POLYPHAGIA.rationale: Polyphagia occurs because cells cannot use glucose. Weight loss despite eating more is a type 1 clue; it is not explained by a sulfonylurea, which more often increases weight through insulin release.

RETINOPATHY.clue: Microvascular eye disease of diabetes found on a dilated exam before vision is lost
RETINOPATHY.rationale: Schedule periodic dilated retinal exams; the interval depends on findings and pregnancy, not on symptoms. Rapid improvement in glucose can temporarily worsen retinopathy; controlling blood pressure and glucose slows progression; new floaters or vision loss need same-day eye care.

NEUROPATHY.clue: Nerve damage that in diabetes is usually stocking-glove sensory loss and raises ulcer risk
NEUROPATHY.rationale: Check the feet at visits and teach daily inspection and proper shoes. Painful neuropathy is treated with duloxetine, pregabalin, or gabapentin, not with opioids first; sudden asymmetric pain suggests a different neuropathy that needs another workup.

NEPHROPATHY.clue: Kidney disease of diabetes detected by urine albumin and a falling filtration rate
NEPHROPATHY.rationale: An ACE inhibitor or ARB is used when albuminuria is present and blood pressure allows. An SGLT2 inhibitor slows progression of chronic kidney disease with or without diabetes when the indication is met; do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.

ALBUMINURIA.clue: Urine protein leak that marks diabetic kidney disease and favors an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin-receptor blocker
ALBUMINURIA.rationale: Confirm albuminuria with a repeat sample because fever, exercise, and menstruation can raise it. Treat blood pressure and glucose, and add an SGLT2 inhibitor when kidney and heart indications apply; non-dihydropyridine calcium blockers are not a substitute for renin-angiotensin blockade here.

ACIDOSIS.clue: Fall in blood pH; the anion-gap form with ketones is diabetic ketoacidosis
ACIDOSIS.rationale: Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation. Other anion-gap causes include lactic acidosis, toxins, and kidney failure; metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare and linked to severe kidney failure or tissue hypoxia, not to routine use.

SOMOGYI.clue: Morning hyperglycemia that follows unrecognized overnight hypoglycemia
SOMOGYI.rationale: A low glucose in the middle of the night distinguishes the Somogyi effect from the dawn phenomenon, which is a hormone-driven rise without preceding hypoglycemia. The overnight low is treated by reducing the evening insulin, not by adding more.

DAWN.clue: Early-morning hyperglycemia from counter-regulatory hormones, without preceding nocturnal hypoglycemia
DAWN.rationale: The dawn phenomenon is managed by adjusting basal insulin or timing, after a middle-of-the-night glucose shows that the person is not going low. It is the opposite pattern from rebound after an overnight low.

FOOT.clue: Site examined at diabetes visits because neuropathy and poor perfusion allow ulcers to form unnoticed
FOOT.rationale: Look between the toes, test sensation, and check pulses and skin. A hot, red foot without an ulcer can be Charcot change and needs non-weight-bearing and urgent evaluation, not just antibiotics; refer ulcers that are deep, infected, or ischemic.

ULCER.clue: Open sore; on a diabetic foot it is an emergency of pressure, neuropathy, and sometimes ischemia or infection
ULCER.rationale: Offload a plantar foot ulcer and probe for bone. Osteomyelitis is likely when bone is visible or the ulcer is chronic and deep; do not assume a venous stasis ulcer and a neuropathic ulcer need the same dressing plan.

THYROID.clue: Gland whose underactivity raises TSH and whose overactivity suppresses it
THYROID.rationale: Order TSH first for most thyroid complaints. Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and constipation suggest hypothyroidism; weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, and new atrial fibrillation suggest hyperthyroidism; a nodule workup also starts with TSH.

TSH.clue: Pituitary hormone that is high in primary hypothyroidism and low in hyperthyroidism
TSH.rationale: Recheck TSH about six weeks after a thyroxine dose change, because that is when a new steady state is reached. A low TSH with a low free T4 suggests central disease; do not replace thyroid hormone until adrenal insufficiency is considered.

THYROXINE.clue: Oral T4 replacement for hypothyroidism, taken on an empty stomach and separated from calcium and iron
THYROXINE.rationale: Levothyroxine is synthetic thyroxine. Dose requirements usually rise as soon as pregnancy is confirmed; biotin can distort thyroid labs; over-replacement causes atrial fibrillation and bone loss, so treat to the TSH, not to a maximal dose.

GRAVES.clue: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism with a diffuse gland and possible eye disease
GRAVES.rationale: Graves disease shows a low TSH, high free T4, and TSH-receptor antibodies. Beta blockers treat symptoms; methimazole is the usual antithyroid drug except in the first trimester, when propylthiouracil is preferred; radioiodine and surgery are definitive options outside pregnancy.

METHIMAZOLE.clue: Preferred antithyroid drug except in the first trimester, when it is avoided because of birth defects
METHIMAZOLE.rationale: Methimazole can cause agranulocytosis, so fever or sore throat needs an urgent blood count and the drug is stopped. It is teratogenic early in pregnancy; propylthiouracil is used in that window but has more liver toxicity with longer use.

PTU.clue: Antithyroid drug used in the first trimester and in thyroid storm; liver injury limits routine long-term use
PTU.rationale: Propylthiouracil blocks new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. Hepatotoxicity can be severe; after the first trimester, patients are often switched to methimazole; agranulocytosis is still a risk.

GOITER.clue: Enlarged thyroid that can be diffuse in Graves disease or lumpy with nodules
GOITER.rationale: A goiter with compressive symptoms, hoarseness, or rapid growth needs imaging and referral. TSH decides whether a nodule is scanned for uptake or considered for biopsy; most nodules are benign, but red flags are not watched passively.

NODULE.clue: Focal thyroid lesion; TSH is the first test, and ultrasound guides which ones need a needle biopsy
NODULE.rationale: A low TSH suggests a hyperfunctioning nodule and leads to an uptake scan rather than an immediate biopsy. Normal or high TSH leads to ultrasound risk stratification; hoarseness, fixation, and lymphadenopathy are concerning features.

STORM.clue: Life-threatening thyrotoxicosis with fever, delirium, and tachycardia
STORM.rationale: Thyroid storm is an emergency, often triggered by illness, surgery, or stopping an antithyroid drug. Treatment blocks synthesis, blocks release, blocks conversion, and supports the heart; do not give iodine until antithyroid drug has been started.

ADDISON.clue: Primary adrenal insufficiency with hyperpigmentation, salt craving, low sodium, and high potassium
ADDISON.rationale: Addison disease has a low cortisol and a high ACTH. Illness can precipitate crisis, which needs intravenous fluid and a stress-dose steroid; secondary adrenal insufficiency usually lacks hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia because mineralocorticoid is preserved.

CORTISOL.clue: Adrenal hormone that is low in adrenal insufficiency and high in Cushing syndrome
CORTISOL.rationale: A morning cortisol and a cosyntropin stimulation test evaluate deficiency. Cushing screening uses a late-night salivary cortisol, a 24-hour urine cortisol, or a low-dose dexamethasone suppression test; exogenous steroids are the most common cause of the Cushing appearance.

COSYNTROPIN.clue: Synthetic ACTH used to test whether the adrenal glands can release cortisol
COSYNTROPIN.rationale: A cosyntropin stimulation test that fails to raise cortisol supports adrenal insufficiency. It does not by itself separate pituitary from adrenal causes; ACTH level and electrolytes do that; do not delay treatment of crisis for the test.

CUSHING.clue: Syndrome of cortisol excess with central weight gain, purple striae, proximal weakness, and high glucose
CUSHING.rationale: The most common cause is prescribed glucocorticoid. Endogenous disease is screened, then imaged after it is biochemically confirmed; hypertension, osteoporosis, and infection risk accompany the appearance.

STRIAE.clue: Purple, wide stretch marks of Cushing syndrome, unlike the pale marks of ordinary weight change
STRIAE.rationale: Violaceous striae, easy bruising, and proximal weakness suggest cortisol excess rather than simple obesity. Ask about inhaled, injected, and topical steroids as well as oral ones.

BUFFALO.clue: Dorsocervical fat pad associated with cortisol excess
BUFFALO.rationale: A buffalo hump with moon facies and supraclavicular fat supports Cushing syndrome when weakness and purple striae are also present. Ordinary central weight gain lacks the catabolic skin and muscle findings.

ACROMEGALY.clue: Growth-hormone excess in adults that enlarges the hands, jaw, and feet and can cause diabetes
ACROMEGALY.rationale: Screen with insulin-like growth factor 1. A pituitary macroadenoma can cause headache and bitemporal visual-field loss; sleep apnea, carpal tunnel, and colon polyps are associated; refer rather than attributing the changes to aging.

PITUITARY.clue: Gland whose adenoma can secrete prolactin or growth hormone or compress the optic chiasm
PITUITARY.rationale: Bitemporal hemianopsia is the field cut of chiasmal compression. A prolactin elevation needs medication review, pregnancy testing, and TSH before an MRI, because hypothyroidism and antipsychotics raise prolactin; surgery or medical therapy depends on the hormone.

PROLACTIN.clue: Hormone that rises with a pituitary adenoma, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, and many antipsychotics
PROLACTIN.rationale: Galactorrhea and amenorrhea or infertility are the usual clues. Repeat a mildly high level and exclude pregnancy and low thyroid function; dopamine agonists treat most prolactinomas; a very high level suggests a macroadenoma.

HEMIANOPSIA.clue: Loss of half the visual field; the bitemporal pattern points to the optic chiasm
HEMIANOPSIA.rationale: A pituitary mass is the classic cause of bitemporal hemianopsia. Ask about headache, galactorrhea, and changes in ring or shoe size; formal fields and imaging come before reassurance.

SIADH.clue: Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone with low sodium, concentrated urine, and high urine sodium
SIADH.rationale: SIADH is euvolemic hyponatremia. Fluid restriction is first-line when symptoms are mild; causes include medicines, lung disease, and intracranial disease; severe symptoms need urgent hypertonic saline, not free water.

SODIUM.clue: Electrolyte that is low in SIADH and in thiazide use, and that must be corrected carefully to avoid osmotic demyelination
SODIUM.rationale: Chronic hyponatremia is corrected slowly. Thiazides, SSRIs, and carbamazepine are common drug causes; hypernatremia usually means water loss, as in diabetes insipidus, or inadequate access to water.

POTASSIUM.clue: Electrolyte that rises with ACE inhibitors and falls with loop and thiazide diuretics; extremes cause arrhythmia
POTASSIUM.rationale: Do not start insulin for ketoacidosis until potassium is known. Hyperkalemia with an ACE inhibitor plus a mineralocorticoid antagonist needs a lower dose or a different plan; succinylcholine and missed dialysis are acute-care causes of a high value.

CALCIUM.clue: Mineral that is low in hypoparathyroidism and vitamin D deficiency and high in hyperparathyroidism and some cancers
CALCIUM.rationale: Correct calcium for albumin or measure an ionized level. Chvostek and Trousseau signs suggest hypocalcemia; thiazides raise calcium and loops lower it; separate oral calcium from thyroid hormone and from fluoroquinolones.

CHVOSTEK.clue: Facial twitch when the facial nerve is tapped, a sign of low calcium
CHVOSTEK.rationale: Chvostek sign supports hypocalcemia but is not perfectly specific. Confirm with a laboratory calcium; treat symptomatic tetany with intravenous calcium and find the cause, including magnesium deficiency and hypoparathyroidism.

TROUSSEAU.clue: Carpal spasm when a blood-pressure cuff is inflated, a sign of low calcium
TROUSSEAU.rationale: Trousseau sign is more specific for hypocalcemia than the facial twitch. Inflate the cuff above systolic pressure and watch the hand; replace calcium and correct magnesium if it is low.

MAGNESIUM.clue: Mineral given to prevent seizures in preeclampsia; loss of reflexes is the first sign of toxicity
MAGNESIUM.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is continued for a period after delivery because postpartum seizures still occur. Toxicity progresses from lost deep-tendon reflexes to respiratory depression; calcium gluconate is the antidote; loops and diarrhea waste magnesium.

PHOSPHATE.clue: Electrolyte that falls when a malnourished person is refed and that rises in kidney failure
PHOSPHATE.rationale: Refeeding syndrome can drop phosphate, potassium, and magnesium and cause weakness or arrhythmia. Chronic kidney disease raises phosphate, which is treated with diet and binders; always interpret calcium and phosphate together.

PARATHYROID.clue: Glands that raise calcium; a benign adenoma is the usual cause of primary hyperparathyroidism
PARATHYROID.rationale: Primary hyperparathyroidism shows high or high-normal calcium with a PTH that is not suppressed. Many patients are found on routine labs; stones, bone loss, and significant hypercalcemia are reasons to refer for surgery.

OSTEOPENIA.clue: Bone density between normal and osteoporosis, followed with risk calculation rather than automatic drug therapy
OSTEOPENIA.rationale: Osteopenia is a T-score between -1 and -2.5. Fracture risk tools, age, and prior fracture decide who needs medicine; calcium, vitamin D if deficient, and fall prevention apply to everyone in this range.

FRACTURE.clue: A broken bone from a standing fall is treated as osteoporosis until another cause is clear
FRACTURE.rationale: A hip or vertebral fracture from a standing fall warrants treatment discussion even when the density score is not in the osteoporosis range. Rule out pathologic fracture when the story does not match the injury.

ALENDRONATE.clue: Oral bisphosphonate taken upright with water on an empty stomach to prevent esophageal injury
ALENDRONATE.rationale: Alendronate reduces hip and vertebral fractures. Remain upright with water on an empty stomach for at least 30 minutes, avoid it if the person cannot sit up or has severe esophageal disease, and reassess the need after several years of bone-density follow-up.

VITAMIND.clue: Fat-soluble vitamin repleted when it is low and when osteoporosis is treated; toxicity causes high calcium
VITAMIND.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia and a secondary rise in parathyroid hormone. Correct it before or with bisphosphonate therapy; routine high-dose supplementation for every adult is not required to prevent falls.

KYPHOSIS.clue: Forward curvature of the thoracic spine that can follow vertebral compression fractures
KYPHOSIS.rationale: New kyphosis or height loss suggests silent vertebral fractures and needs density testing and a treatment discussion. Scheuermann disease is a different adolescent cause; sudden severe back pain in an older adult is not dismissed as a strain.

BMI.clue: Weight-for-height index used to classify underweight, overweight, and obesity and to trend weight-related risk
BMI.rationale: Body mass index misses muscle versus fat and is interpreted with waist size, comorbidities, and the exam. A value of 30 or higher is obesity; lifestyle therapy is the base, and medication or surgery is added for selected patients.

WAIST.clue: Circumference that reflects central adiposity and cardiometabolic risk beyond weight alone
WAIST.rationale: A large waist with normal body mass index still raises metabolic risk. Measure at the iliac crest in a standard way so the number can be compared over time; it does not replace blood pressure, glucose, or lipid assessment.

ORLISTAT.clue: Lipase inhibitor for weight loss that causes oily stools and reduces absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
ORLISTAT.rationale: Orlistat works only with a lower-fat diet. Supplement vitamins A, D, E, and K at a separate time; it is a modest option compared with GLP-1 receptor agonists but has a long safety record and no stimulant effect.

OBESITY.clue: Excess adiposity that is treated with lifestyle therapy and, when indicated, medication or metabolic surgery
OBESITY.rationale: Obesity is a chronic disease, not a willpower failure. GLP-1 receptor agonists produce clinically important weight loss; surgery is considered for severe obesity or for obesity with serious comorbidity; screen for diabetes, sleep apnea, and fatty liver.

OMEPRAZOLE.clue: Proton-pump inhibitor for reflux and ulcer disease; long-term use has nutrient and infection tradeoffs
OMEPRAZOLE.rationale: Omeprazole heals erosive reflux and is part of Helicobacter therapy. Stop it for two weeks before a stool antigen or urea breath test; long-term use is linked to low magnesium, low B12, fracture risk, and Clostridioides difficile.

FAMOTIDINE.clue: Histamine-2 blocker for milder reflux, with fewer drug interactions than a proton-pump inhibitor
FAMOTIDINE.rationale: Famotidine is less potent than a proton-pump inhibitor and can lose effect with continuous use. Reduce the dose when kidney function is low; it is a reasonable acid reducer when a proton-pump inhibitor would interact with clopidogrel.

SUCRALFATE.clue: Ulcer-coating agent that must be separated from other medicines and works poorly if acid is fully suppressed
SUCRALFATE.rationale: Sucralfate can cause constipation and aluminum retention in kidney disease. Give other drugs at a different time; it is not a substitute for treating Helicobacter or for evaluating alarm symptoms.

DYSPEPSIA.clue: Upper-abdominal discomfort; alarm features such as bleeding, anemia, or weight loss need endoscopy rather than a simple acid-reducer trial
DYSPEPSIA.rationale: In younger adults without alarm features, test-and-treat for Helicobacter or a short acid-suppression trial is reasonable. Do not attribute progressive dysphagia or gastrointestinal bleeding to simple dyspepsia.

ENDOSCOPY.clue: Upper-tract scope used for alarm symptoms, bleeding, and complicated ulcer or reflux disease
ENDOSCOPY.rationale: Endoscopy visualizes esophagus, stomach, and duodenum and can treat bleeding. It is not the first test for uncomplicated typical reflux; hold decisions about biopsy for celiac or Helicobacter depend on the indication.

PYLORI.clue: Stomach bacterium that causes peptic ulcer and raises cancer risk; confirm cure after treatment when indicated
PYLORI.rationale: Helicobacter pylori regimens include acid suppression plus multiple antibiotics because single-drug treatment fails. Stop a proton-pump inhibitor before stool antigen or breath testing; quadruple therapy is preferred where clarithromycin resistance is common.

BISMUTH.clue: Agent in multi-drug Helicobacter therapy that blackens the stool and tongue
BISMUTH.rationale: Bismuth is not an antibiotic by itself. The salicylate form is avoided in children because of Reye syndrome concerns; black stool from bismuth should not be mistaken for melena if the rest of the story fits.

MELENA.clue: Black, tarry stool from digested blood, usually an upper gastrointestinal bleed
MELENA.rationale: Melena needs a hemoglobin and a decision about endoscopy, not a hemorrhoid cream. Iron and bismuth can also darken stool but do not make it tarry and foul in the same way; unstable vital signs require emergency care.

HEMATEMESIS.clue: Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, a sign of upper gastrointestinal bleeding
HEMATEMESIS.rationale: Hematemesis is an emergency when volume loss, liver disease, or syncope is present. Two large-bore access points and endoscopy are hospital decisions; do not start the workup with a stool softener.

CELIAC.clue: Immune reaction to gluten causing diarrhea, bloating, and iron deficiency; test before removing gluten
CELIAC.rationale: Order IgA tissue transglutaminase while the person is still eating gluten, and check total IgA because deficiency causes a false negative. Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin form; treatment is lifelong gluten avoidance, with dietitian support.

GLUTEN.clue: Grain protein that must stay in the diet until celiac testing is finished
GLUTEN.rationale: Starting a gluten-free diet before serology or biopsy can make celiac disease impossible to confirm. Wheat, barley, and rye are the sources that matter; oats are tolerated by many if they are not contaminated.

CROHN.clue: Inflammatory bowel disease with skip lesions anywhere from mouth to anus and a risk of fistula
CROHN.rationale: Crohn disease can present with pain, nonbloody diarrhea, weight loss, and perianal disease. Steroids treat flares but are not maintenance; refer for steroid-sparing therapy rather than repeating short courses.

COLITIS.clue: Colon inflammation; the ulcerative form starts at the rectum and causes bloody diarrhea
COLITIS.rationale: Ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum, unlike Crohn skip lesions, and mesalamine is used for mild to moderate disease. Antibiotic-associated colitis from Clostridioides difficile, especially after clindamycin, needs stool testing rather than an antimotility drug, and soap-and-water handwashing because alcohol gel does not kill spores.

MESALAMINE.clue: Aminosalicylate used to induce and maintain remission in mild to moderate ulcerative colitis
MESALAMINE.rationale: Mesalamine delivery site matters, so the formulation is matched to disease location. It is not sufficient therapy for moderate to severe Crohn disease of the small bowel; watch for idiosyncratic kidney injury and for worsening colitis.

FISTULA.clue: Abnormal tract between bowel and skin, bladder, or vagina, a complication of Crohn disease
FISTULA.rationale: A fistula with fever or abscess needs drainage and specialist care, not another course of an antidiarrheal. Perianal pain in known inflammatory bowel disease should be examined rather than assumed to be a fissure only.

DIVERTICULA.clue: Colonic outpouchings that can inflame and cause left-lower-quadrant pain and fever
DIVERTICULA.rationale: Stable uncomplicated diverticulitis in an immunocompetent adult is sometimes managed without antibiotics. Perforation, abscess, sepsis, or immunosuppression needs urgent imaging and treatment; a fiber-rich diet is used for prevention after recovery, not during acute severe pain.

QUADRANT.clue: Abdominal region; right-upper pain that stops inspiration suggests gallbladder inflammation
QUADRANT.rationale: Right-lower pain with migration from the umbilicus suggests appendicitis. Left-lower pain and fever suggest diverticulitis; suprapubic pain with urinary symptoms suggests cystitis; always consider ectopic pregnancy in a person who can be pregnant.

MURPHY.clue: Inspiratory arrest during right-upper-quadrant palpation, a bedside sign of acute cholecystitis
MURPHY.rationale: A positive Murphy sign supports gallbladder inflammation but does not replace ultrasound. Keep the patient from eating and drinking if surgery is likely; fever plus jaundice plus right-upper pain is cholangitis, which is more urgent.

CHARCOT.clue: Triad of right-upper pain, fever, and jaundice that indicates ascending cholangitis
CHARCOT.rationale: Charcot triad plus hypotension and confusion is Reynolds pentad and is a biliary emergency. Do not manage it as simple biliary colic; antibiotics and biliary decompression are hospital care.

GALLSTONE.clue: Biliary calculus that causes colic after fatty meals and can obstruct the cystic or common duct
GALLSTONE.rationale: Biliary colic is episodic and resolves; cholecystitis persists with fever and a positive Murphy sign. Pancreatitis occurs when a stone passes through the common channel; asymptomatic stones found incidentally usually do not need removal.

LIPASE.clue: Pancreatic enzyme that is more specific than amylase for acute pancreatitis
LIPASE.rationale: Epigastric pain boring to the back with nausea suggests pancreatitis. Common causes are gallstones, alcohol, very high triglycerides, and medicines; aggressive early fluids and finding the cause matter more than a special diet on day one.

AMYLASE.clue: Pancreatic enzyme that rises in pancreatitis but is less specific than lipase
AMYLASE.rationale: Amylase can come from salivary glands and returns to normal sooner than lipase. Do not exclude pancreatitis on one normal amylase if the story and lipase fit; chronic pancreatitis may show little enzyme rise.

CULLEN.clue: Periumbilical bruising that can appear with hemorrhagic pancreatitis
CULLEN.rationale: Cullen sign is late and uncommon. Grey Turner flank bruising has the same meaning; neither is required to diagnose pancreatitis, and their absence is not reassuring in a sick patient.

TURNER.clue: Flank bruising associated with hemorrhagic pancreatitis
TURNER.rationale: Grey Turner sign, like periumbilical bruising, suggests retroperitoneal bleeding. It is not an early finding; unstable abdominal pain still needs emergency care without waiting for skin changes.

JAUNDICE.clue: Yellow skin and sclera from elevated bilirubin; painless yellowing in an older adult is a cancer concern
JAUNDICE.rationale: Jaundice with dark urine and pale stool suggests conjugated obstruction. Fever and right-upper pain suggest cholangitis; painless progressive jaundice needs urgent imaging, not a watch-and-wait plan.

BILIRUBIN.clue: Pigment from heme breakdown; the conjugated form appears in urine when the liver or bile duct is obstructed
BILIRUBIN.rationale: Unconjugated elevation is seen in hemolysis and Gilbert syndrome, and the urine stays clear. Conjugated elevation darkens urine; neonatal bilirubin is interpreted with age in hours and risk factors, not with one adult normal range.

HEPATITIS.clue: Liver inflammation; A is fecal-oral and vaccine-preventable, B and C are blood-borne, and only C lacks a vaccine
HEPATITIS.rationale: Hepatitis B surface antigen means infection, and surface antibody means immunity. Hepatitis C is often curable with direct-acting antivirals and is screened in adults without using a changing age cutoff as the only clue; acute hepatitis A does not become chronic.

CIRRHOSIS.clue: End-stage liver scarring with spider angiomas, ascites, varices, and the risk of encephalopathy
CIRRHOSIS.rationale: Stop alcohol, vaccinate against hepatitis A and B if nonimmune, and avoid NSAIDs. Nonselective beta blockers are used for varices, lactulose for encephalopathy, and salt restriction plus diuretics for ascites; screen for liver cancer in eligible patients.

ASCITES.clue: Fluid in the abdomen from portal hypertension; a fever with it may be spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
