ASCITES.rationale: New ascites needs a diagnostic tap. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is treated even when the person does not look dramatically ill; salt restriction, spironolactone, and a loop diuretic are the usual outpatient measures for cirrhotic fluid.

VARICES.clue: Dilated portosystemic veins that can bleed massively; nonselective beta blockers help prevent bleeding
VARICES.rationale: Hematemesis in cirrhosis is variceal until proven otherwise and is an emergency. Do not use NSAIDs; after a bleed, secondary prevention combines a beta blocker with endoscopic therapy.

AMMONIA.clue: Toxin that rises in hepatic encephalopathy, treated with lactulose rather than with protein starvation
AMMONIA.rationale: Lactulose is titrated to a few soft stools a day, and rifaximin is added for recurrent encephalopathy. Do not restrict protein so severely that the person becomes malnourished; find a trigger such as infection, bleeding, or a sedative.

LACTULOSE.clue: Nonabsorbable sugar that lowers ammonia by trapping it in the gut
LACTULOSE.rationale: Lactulose is first-line for hepatic encephalopathy. Titrate to roughly two to three soft stools daily and watch for dehydration and electrolyte loss; it is also an osmotic laxative for constipation.

PORTAL.clue: Venous system whose hypertension causes varices, splenomegaly, and ascites
PORTAL.rationale: Portal hypertension is the circulatory consequence of cirrhosis. A new gastrointestinal bleed, confusion, or fever in this setting is urgent; nonselective beta blockers lower portal pressure.

HEMORRHOID.clue: Dilated anal cushion that causes bright red blood on paper; darker blood or anemia still needs a cancer evaluation
HEMORRHOID.rationale: Fiber, stool softening, and sitz baths treat most symptomatic hemorrhoids. Thrombosed external hemorrhoids are acutely painful; do not blame every rectal bleed on hemorrhoids when age, weight loss, or a change in stool is present.

FIBER.clue: Dietary bulk that softens stool and is first-line for ordinary constipation and hemorrhoid prevention
FIBER.rationale: Increase fiber with fluid, or bloating worsens. It helps irritable bowel constipation and diverticular prevention; it is not the treatment of opioid ileus, obstruction, or severe inflammatory colitis.

SENNA.clue: Stimulant laxative used when bulk and osmotic agents are not enough
SENNA.rationale: Senna produces a bowel movement within hours and can cramp. It is appropriate short term and with opioids; do not use a stimulant when bowel obstruction is possible.

BISACODYL.clue: Stimulant laxative similar to senna, avoided when obstruction or severe cramping is present
BISACODYL.rationale: Bisacodyl is used for occasional constipation and bowel preparation, not as the first step before fiber and an osmotic agent. Chronic daily stimulant use is a reason to look for a cause rather than to escalate forever.

DOCUSATE.clue: Stool softener with modest evidence, sometimes paired with a stimulant when stools are hard
DOCUSATE.rationale: Docusate alone often disappoints. Opioid constipation responds better to a stimulant plus an osmotic agent, or to a peripheral antagonist if laxatives fail; softeners do not treat obstruction.

LOPERAMIDE.clue: Antimotility drug that is unsafe in bloody diarrhea, high fever, or suspected C. difficile
LOPERAMIDE.rationale: Loperamide is acceptable for simple watery diarrhea and for some irritable-bowel diarrhea. It can cause cardiac arrhythmia in overdose; do not use it in invasive bacterial gastroenteritis or in young children with dysentery.

ONDANSETRON.clue: Antinausea medicine that can prolong the QT interval and is not first-line for nausea of pregnancy
ONDANSETRON.rationale: First-line treatment of nausea in pregnancy is doxylamine plus pyridoxine. Ondansetron is a later option; headache and constipation are common, and other QT-prolonging drugs raise the rhythm risk.

GIARDIA.clue: Parasite causing foul, prolonged diarrhea after untreated water; stool antigen testing is more useful than one ova exam
GIARDIA.rationale: Giardia is treated with metronidazole, tinidazole, or nitazoxanide. Household contacts with symptoms should be tested; it does not cause bloody invasive diarrhea the way some bacteria do.

IBS.clue: Disorder of pain with bowel-habit change and no alarm features such as bleeding, anemia, or nocturnal symptoms
IBS.rationale: Irritable bowel syndrome is a positive clinical diagnosis after limited evaluation, not a label for every abdominal pain. Fiber or an osmotic laxative helps constipation-predominant disease; fever, weight loss, or blood requires a different workup.

UTI.clue: Urinary infection; uncomplicated bladder infection is treated with a short course, while kidney infection is not
UTI.rationale: Nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole when resistance is low, or fosfomycin treats uncomplicated cystitis. Nitrofurantoin does not reach kidney tissue, so it is wrong for pyelonephritis; in pregnancy, treat even asymptomatic bacteriuria.

CYSTITIS.clue: Bladder infection with dysuria and frequency but without fever or flank pain
CYSTITIS.rationale: Uncomplicated cystitis in a nonpregnant adult can be treated without a culture if resistance patterns are known. Fever, vomiting, or flank pain means pyelonephritis or another diagnosis; a urinary analgesic does not treat the organism and colors urine orange.

DYSURIA.clue: Painful urination from cystitis, urethritis, vaginitis, or herpes, not from infection alone
DYSURIA.rationale: Always consider sexually transmitted infection and vaginal disease when the urine is bland. Phenazopyridine eases symptoms for a day or two, stains urine orange, and is not an antibiotic; pregnancy with dysuria needs a culture.

FREQUENCY.clue: Urinary symptom of infection, overactive bladder, prostate enlargement, or high glucose
FREQUENCY.rationale: Frequency with dysuria suggests cystitis. Frequency with urgency and little urine suggests overactive bladder; frequency with large volumes suggests diabetes or diabetes insipidus; nocturia in an older man suggests prostate or heart failure or sleep apnea.

URGENCY.clue: Sudden need to void that defines urge incontinence and also occurs with bladder infection
URGENCY.rationale: Urge incontinence is treated with bladder training first. Antimuscarinic drugs such as oxybutynin cause dry mouth and confusion and are poor choices in older adults; mirabegron is a beta-3 agonist alternative that can raise blood pressure.

HEMATURIA.clue: Blood in the urine that is never blamed on a urinary infection until the culture proves one and the blood clears
HEMATURIA.rationale: Gross hematuria, especially without pain, needs evaluation for malignancy in adults. Clots and colic suggest a stone; tea-colored urine after a sore throat suggests glomerulonephritis; confirm that the dipstick is not just myoglobin.

NITRITE.clue: Urine finding produced by many gram-negative bacteria; a negative result does not exclude infection
NITRITE.rationale: Nitrite supports Enterobacterales infection but misses enterococcus and some other organisms that do not reduce nitrate. Leukocyte esterase is more sensitive and less specific; symptoms still decide whether a culture is needed.

PYURIA.clue: White cells in the urine that support inflammation but do not by themselves prove a bacterial infection
PYURIA.rationale: Pyuria without bacteria occurs with urethritis, vaginitis, and interstitial cystitis. Sterile pyuria also occurs with tuberculosis and some sexually transmitted infections; treat the syndrome, not the cells alone.

LEUKOCYTE.clue: White cell whose esterase on a dipstick supports urinary inflammation
LEUKOCYTE.rationale: Leukocyte esterase plus symptoms supports cystitis, especially with nitrite. Contamination from vaginal discharge causes false positives; a catheter specimen is more reliable when the clean-catch is equivocal.

CULTURE.clue: Urine test required for pregnancy, recurrent infection, pyelonephritis, and treatment failure
CULTURE.rationale: Uncomplicated cystitis in a nonpregnant woman does not always need a culture before a guideline short course. Men, children, and pregnant patients do; always culture before treating pyelonephritis so the drug can be narrowed.

FOSFOMYCIN.clue: Single-dose antibiotic option for uncomplicated cystitis, not for kidney infection
FOSFOMYCIN.rationale: Fosfomycin covers many resistant bladder organisms but does not treat pyelonephritis. It is useful when adherence to a longer course is unlikely; it is not the drug for complicated or upper-tract disease.

BACTERIURIA.clue: Bacteria in the urine without symptoms; treat this in pregnancy, not in healthy nonpregnant adults
BACTERIURIA.rationale: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults and in people with catheters is not treated, because antibiotics cause harm without benefit. Pregnancy is the major outpatient exception, along with some urologic procedures; a positive dipstick without symptoms is not a reason to prescribe.

FLANK.clue: Lateral back pain that, with fever and urinary symptoms, means pyelonephritis rather than simple cystitis
FLANK.rationale: Pyelonephritis needs a culture and an antibiotic that reaches kidney tissue, not nitrofurantoin. Pregnancy, vomiting, sepsis, or a possible stone with obstruction needs emergency care; image if the person is very ill or not improving.

CREATININE.clue: Muscle-breakdown product used to estimate filtration; a rise means the kidney is worsening
CREATININE.rationale: Compare creatinine with the person's baseline, not only with the lab reference range. ACE inhibitors can raise it slightly; a large rise, hyperkalemia, or oliguria is acute kidney injury and medicine doses must be reviewed.

CKD.clue: Chronic loss of filtration that changes drug doses and makes an ACE inhibitor or SGLT2 inhibitor useful when albumin is leaking
CKD.rationale: Chronic kidney disease is defined by a low filtration rate or by markers such as albuminuria lasting at least three months. Avoid NSAIDs, adjust metformin and many antibiotics, and do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB; an SGLT2 inhibitor slows progression in eligible patients.

AKI.clue: Abrupt drop in kidney function from low volume, a nephrotoxin, or obstruction
AKI.rationale: Acute kidney injury is prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal. Stop NSAIDs and review ACE inhibitors, diuretics, and antibiotics; a distended bladder means relieve obstruction; do not give potassium while the kidney is failing.

CAST.clue: Urinary cylinder; muddy-brown granular forms suggest tubular injury and red-cell forms suggest glomerulonephritis
CAST.rationale: White-cell casts suggest pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis. Hyaline casts are nonspecific; the dipstick does not replace microscopy when glomerular disease is possible.

PROTEINURIA.clue: Protein in the urine that, with new hypertension after mid-pregnancy, supports preeclampsia
PROTEINURIA.rationale: Diabetic albuminuria is a reason for an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker. Transient protein appears with fever and exercise, so confirm a persistent result; heavy protein with edema suggests nephrotic syndrome and needs more than a repeat dipstick.

STONE.clue: Ureteral calculus causing colic that radiates to the groin; strain urine and force fluids if the person can keep them down
STONE.rationale: Most small distal stones pass. Fever with an obstructing stone is an emergency because of infected hydronephrosis; alpha blockers are sometimes used to help a distal stone pass; recurrent stones need a metabolic evaluation, not just another pain prescription.

CALCULUS.clue: Another word for a kidney stone; calcium stones are the most common and are not treated by restricting all dietary calcium
CALCULUS.rationale: Normal dietary calcium with food binds oxalate in the gut. Very high sodium and animal protein increase stone risk; hydration is the intervention that helps almost every stone former.

BPH.clue: Benign prostate enlargement causing weak stream, hesitancy, and nocturia
BPH.rationale: An alpha blocker such as tamsulosin works within days but does not shrink the gland. A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor shrinks the gland over months and lowers PSA, so interpret the antigen with that effect in mind; refer for retention, recurrent infection, or a suspicious prostate exam.

TAMSULOSIN.clue: Alpha blocker that eases prostate symptoms quickly and can cause floppy iris during later cataract surgery
TAMSULOSIN.rationale: Tamsulosin does not lower PSA or shrink the prostate. Take it at night if dizziness occurs; tell the eye surgeon about current or past use before cataract extraction; it is not a blood-pressure drug of choice.

FINASTERIDE.clue: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that shrinks the prostate over months and lowers the PSA value
FINASTERIDE.rationale: Finasteride takes months to help urinary symptoms and can cause sexual side effects. Pregnant people should not handle crushed tablets because it is teratogenic, and the measured PSA is roughly halved while the drug is taken.

PSA.clue: Prostate antigen used to follow known disease and, after shared decision-making, to screen selected men
PSA.rationale: PSA is not a mandatory test at one fixed age. Finasteride and dutasteride lower it; a rising value, a nodule, or unexplained bone pain needs referral even if a past value was reassuring; urinary infection can temporarily raise it.

NOCTURIA.clue: Waking to urinate, from prostate enlargement, overactive bladder, edema states, or sleep apnea
NOCTURIA.rationale: Nighttime frequency with a weak stream suggests benign prostatic hyperplasia. Leg edema that returns to the circulation at night causes nocturia that a bladder drug will not fix; ask about snoring and blood pressure medicines taken in the evening.

SILDENAFIL.clue: PDE5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction that must not be combined with any nitrate
SILDENAFIL.rationale: Sildenafil can cause headache, flushing, and a blue visual tint. Separate it from a nitrate by a sufficient interval, longer for the daily longer-acting drug in the class; assess cardiovascular risk before prescribing, because erectile dysfunction is a vascular marker.

TADALAFIL.clue: Longer-acting PDE5 inhibitor also used for prostate symptoms; nitrates remain contraindicated
TADALAFIL.rationale: Tadalafil lasts longer than sildenafil, so the nitrate-free interval is longer. Daily low-dose use treats both erectile dysfunction and lower urinary symptoms; sudden vision or hearing loss means stop the drug and evaluate.

NITRATE.clue: Anti-anginal vasodilator that causes dangerous hypotension if a PDE5 inhibitor is also present
NITRATE.rationale: Nitrates and sildenafil, tadalafil, or vardenafil must not be combined. A long-acting nitrate plus hydralazine is used in selected heart-failure patients; headache and tolerance are common; a nitrate-free interval reduces tolerance.

ERECTILE.clue: Sexual function that fails from vascular disease, medicines, hormones, or psychologic causes
ERECTILE.rationale: Erectile dysfunction prompts a cardiovascular risk review, not only a PDE5 inhibitor. Check morning testosterone when libido is low or the exam suggests hypogonadism, and confirm a low value; depression, alcohol, and beta blockers are reversible contributors.

LIBIDO.clue: Sexual desire; loss of it with erectile dysfunction suggests a hormone, mood, or medicine cause rather than a purely vascular one
LIBIDO.rationale: SSRIs commonly reduce libido. Low morning testosterone confirmed on a second test, with symptoms, is the setting for replacement; replacing testosterone in a eugonadal man does not fix vascular erectile dysfunction and suppresses fertility.

PRIAPISM.clue: Prolonged painful erection that is an emergency; trazodone and sickle cell disease are classic causes
PRIAPISM.rationale: Ischemic priapism needs urgent decompression, not observation overnight. PDE5 inhibitors rarely cause it; recurrent stuttering episodes in sickle cell disease need a hematology plan as well as acute care.

TORSION.clue: Twisting of the testis that causes sudden pain and nausea and cannot wait for imaging if suspicion is high
TORSION.rationale: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency measured in hours. The cremasteric reflex is often absent and the testis may sit high; epididymitis is more gradual and comes with urinary or sexual-exposure clues; do not delay a likely torsion for a routine ultrasound slot.

CREMASTERIC.clue: Reflex that lifts the testis when the inner thigh is stroked and is often absent in torsion
CREMASTERIC.rationale: An absent cremasteric reflex supports torsion but a present reflex does not fully exclude it when the story is sudden and severe. Compare sides; nausea with abrupt scrotal pain is torsion until a surgeon says otherwise.

TESTICLE.clue: Gonad; a painless solid mass is cancer until proven otherwise and is not biopsied through the scrotum
TESTICLE.rationale: Testicular cancer occurs in young adults. The operation is a radical inguinal orchiectomy, not a trans-scrotal biopsy; alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin help with germ-cell tumors; teach monthly self-exam without creating panic over every transient ache.

HYDROCELE.clue: Fluid around the testis that transilluminates and is usually painless
HYDROCELE.rationale: A hydrocele shines with a light. A solid mass does not; a new hydrocele in a young adult still deserves an exam for an underlying tumor; infants with a communicating hydrocele are observed or referred based on persistence.

VARICOCELE.clue: Bag-of-worms dilation of the pampiniform plexus, usually on the left, that can impair fertility
VARICOCELE.rationale: A varicocele decompresses when the person lies down. A right-sided or non-decompressing varicocele needs imaging for a retroperitoneal mass; it does not transilluminate the way a hydrocele does.

SEMINOMA.clue: Germ-cell testicular tumor that is highly curable when found as a painless mass
SEMINOMA.rationale: Seminoma is one histologic type; mixed and nonseminomatous tumors also present as a painless nodule. Any solid intratesticular mass is referred urgently; delay for a course of antibiotics is a common error when infection is not actually present.

EPIDIDYMIS.clue: Structure behind the testis that inflames gradually, often from a sexually transmitted infection in younger men
EPIDIDYMIS.rationale: Epididymitis is tender along the posterior testis and may improve with scrotal elevation. Cover gonorrhea and chlamydia in sexually active younger men, and enteric organisms in older men; sudden onset with nausea is torsion, not epididymitis.

PROSTATITIS.clue: Prostate infection with fever, perineal pain, and a very tender gland that should not be massaged vigorously
PROSTATITIS.rationale: Acute bacterial prostatitis can seed the blood if the gland is manipulated. Culture the urine and treat for several weeks; chronic pelvic pain without infection is a different syndrome and does not improve with endless antibiotics.

PHIMOSIS.clue: Tight foreskin that cannot be retracted; the emergency is the retracted form that will not return and swells
PHIMOSIS.rationale: Physiologic nonretraction is normal in young boys and should not be forced. Pathologic phimosis in adults can be treated with a topical steroid or surgery; paraphimosis, with a trapped retracted foreskin, is ischemic and needs immediate reduction.

SCROTAL.clue: Pouch whose sudden severe pain is torsion until proven otherwise
SCROTAL.rationale: Examine the abdomen too, because retrocecal appendicitis and a ureteral stone can refer to the scrotum. Transilluminate a painless swelling; a fever with a tender epididymis is infection; a painless hard mass is tumor.

DOXYCYCLINE.clue: Tetracycline used for early Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever at any age, chlamydia, and some skin infections
DOXYCYCLINE.rationale: Doxycycline is preferred for uncomplicated chlamydia and is the drug for Rocky Mountain spotted fever even in children. Prolonged tetracycline exposure is avoided in pregnancy and in young children because it can stain developing teeth; take it with water and stay upright, and counsel about sun sensitivity.

AMOXICILLIN.clue: Aminopenicillin that is first-line for strep throat and for many cases of acute otitis media and outpatient pneumonia in healthy adults
AMOXICILLIN.rationale: Amoxicillin does not cover beta-lactamase producers, so sinusitis and animal bites usually need the clavulanate combination. Avoid it when mononucleosis is likely because a rash is common and is not a lifelong allergy; it is not adequate alone for gonorrhea.

CEPHALEXIN.clue: First-generation cephalosporin for streptococcal cellulitis and for many skin infections when methicillin-sensitive staph is likely
CEPHALEXIN.rationale: Cephalexin does not cover MRSA. Purulent abscesses need drainage and often an MRSA-active drug; a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin makes a cephalosporin a poor choice; a remote mild rash usually does not.

CEFTRIAXONE.clue: Intramuscular cephalosporin used for gonorrhea and as part of outpatient pelvic inflammatory disease treatment
CEFTRIAXONE.rationale: Ceftriaxone dose for gonorrhea has changed over time, so use the current regimen rather than a memorized older milligram amount. Add doxycycline when chlamydia has not been excluded; it does not treat syphilis.

CHLAMYDIA.clue: Often silent sexually transmitted bacterium; doxycycline is preferred and partners need treatment
CHLAMYDIA.rationale: Nucleic acid amplification testing is the preferred test. Untreated infection can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy; neonatal eye and lung infection can follow perinatal exposure; retest in a few months because reinfection is common.

GONORRHEA.clue: Sexually transmitted diplococcus treated with ceftriaxone; disseminated disease causes pustules and tenosynovitis
GONORRHEA.rationale: Gonorrhea and chlamydia often travel together, so cover chlamydia unless it has been excluded. Expedited partner therapy is legal in many places; pharyngeal infection is harder to clear and needs a test of cure in the situations current guidance specifies.

SYPHILIS.clue: Spirochete infection whose only reliable treatment in pregnancy is penicillin
SYPHILIS.rationale: Primary syphilis is a painless chancre, and secondary disease includes a rash on palms and soles. Nontreponemal titers follow treatment response; treponemal tests often stay positive for life; neurosyphilis needs a different penicillin regimen; a fever after treatment can be a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

CHANCRE.clue: Painless genital ulcer of primary syphilis
CHANCRE.rationale: A painful ulcer is more often herpes. A chancre is highly infectious and can be missed because it does not hurt; darkfield or serology confirms syphilis, and penicillin is the treatment; examine and treat partners.

HERPES.clue: Recurrent painful vesicles; antiviral therapy shortens outbreaks and daily use reduces transmission
HERPES.rationale: Herpes simplex can shed without lesions. Start acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir at the prodrome; active genital lesions at the time of labor are a reason for cesarean birth; the virus establishes latency, so treatment is not a cure.

ACYCLOVIR.clue: Antiviral for herpes simplex and zoster that is started as early as possible in the outbreak
ACYCLOVIR.rationale: Acyclovir needs more frequent dosing than valacyclovir. Hydrate with higher doses because crystals can injure the kidney; it does not eradicate latency; topical therapy is much less effective for genital disease.

ZOSTER.clue: Dermatomal reactivation of varicella that should be treated early and can threaten the eye if the nose tip is involved
ZOSTER.rationale: Shingles does not cross the midline. Antivirals work best within about three days of the rash, and pain control prevents suffering; Hutchinson sign, vesicles on the tip of the nose, needs urgent eye care; offer recombinant zoster vaccine to older adults on the current schedule.

DERMATOME.clue: Strip of skin supplied by one nerve root; a vesicular rash confined to it is zoster
DERMATOME.rationale: A dermatomal rash that crosses the midline or involves several regions is not typical zoster. Pain can precede the vesicles; postherpetic neuralgia is treated with gabapentin, pregabalin, or a tricyclic, not with continued antiviral therapy alone.

HUTCHINSON.clue: Vesicles on the tip of the nose that mean zoster may involve the eye
HUTCHINSON.rationale: Hutchinson sign reflects nasociliary branch involvement. The eye can scar even when the globe looks quiet at first, so refer urgently; do not rely on an oral antiviral alone without an eye exam.

VARICELLA.clue: Chickenpox, with lesions in several stages at once; aspirin is avoided and pregnant contacts need special prophylaxis
VARICELLA.rationale: Varicella is airborne and contact-spread. Healthy young children are usually supported without an antiviral; adolescents, adults, pregnant people, and immunocompromised patients need antiviral therapy; a nonimmune pregnant contact should receive varicella-zoster immune globulin, not the live vaccine.

PRODROME.clue: Warning symptoms, such as tingling before herpes vesicles or the aura before some migraines
PRODROME.rationale: Starting an antiviral at the herpes prodrome shortens the outbreak. A migraine prodrome is not the same as an aura and does not by itself contraindicate estrogen; teach patients to recognize their own warning so treatment is not delayed.

FLUCONAZOLE.clue: Oral azole for uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis; topical azoles are preferred in pregnancy
FLUCONAZOLE.rationale: Fluconazole inhibits CYP enzymes and raises levels of many drugs, including some statins and warfarin. A single dose treats uncomplicated vaginal yeast; recurrent disease needs a longer plan; it does not treat dermatophyte nail infection as well as terbinafine.

CANDIDA.clue: Yeast that causes cottage-cheese discharge, diaper rash with satellite pustules, and thrush
CANDIDA.rationale: Vaginal candidiasis itches, has a normal pH, and shows hyphae on a potassium hydroxide prep. Topical or oral azoles treat it; nystatin is an alternative on mucosa; satellite pustules distinguish diaper candidiasis from irritant rash, which spares the folds.

WHIFF.clue: Fishy odor released when alkali is added to discharge, supporting bacterial vaginosis
WHIFF.rationale: The whiff test is one Amsel criterion, along with thin gray discharge, pH above 4.5, and clue cells. Three of four criteria diagnose bacterial vaginosis; treat symptomatic disease with metronidazole or clindamycin; trichomonas also can smell strong but shows motile organisms.

CLUE.clue: Epithelial cells coated with bacteria on a saline prep, supporting bacterial vaginosis
CLUE.rationale: Clue cells plus an elevated pH and a positive whiff test confirm bacterial vaginosis under Amsel criteria. They are not seen in typical candidiasis; pregnancy with symptoms is treated; partner treatment guidance has been changing, so follow the current sexually transmitted infection guideline.

TRICHOMONAS.clue: Flagellated sexually transmitted protozoan; treat partners and retest because reinfection is common
TRICHOMONAS.rationale: Trichomonas causes frothy discharge and a strawberry cervix, but many cases are asymptomatic and wet mount misses them. Nucleic acid amplification is more sensitive; metronidazole or tinidazole is used, with multi-day therapy preferred for women; it increases HIV transmission and preterm birth risk.

CLINDAMYCIN.clue: Antibiotic used for bacterial vaginosis and for some MRSA skin infections, with a high risk of C. difficile
CLINDAMYCIN.rationale: Clindamycin covers anaerobes and some gram-positive organisms. Diarrhea during or after it needs Clostridioides difficile testing, not an antimotility drug; it is an alternative for some penicillin-allergic patients when the organism is susceptible.

ECZEMA.clue: Itchy flexural rash of atopic dermatitis; restore the skin barrier and use a topical corticosteroid for flares
ECZEMA.rationale: Eczema care is daily emollient plus a topical steroid of appropriate potency for flares. Face and folds need a low-potency steroid; sedating antihistamines do not treat the rash; topical calcineurin inhibitors are steroid-sparing options; systemic steroids are not routine maintenance.

PSORIASIS.clue: Well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces; nail pitting and joint pain suggest psoriatic arthritis
PSORIASIS.rationale: Auspitz sign is pinpoint bleeding when scale is lifted. Guttate psoriasis can follow strep throat; topical steroids and vitamin D analogues treat limited disease; refer when joints are involved or body surface area is large; systemic steroids can flare pustular disease.

ROSACEA.clue: Centro-facial redness and papules without comedones; topical steroids make it worse
ROSACEA.rationale: Rosacea is triggered by heat, alcohol, and spicy food. Topical metronidazole, ivermectin, or azelaic acid treats papules; eye symptoms need attention because ocular disease can scar the cornea; it is not acne and does not respond to acne antibiotics alone as a plan.

ACNE.clue: Follicular disorder of comedones and inflammatory papules; do not use an antibiotic as the only treatment
ACNE.rationale: First-line acne care combines a topical retinoid with benzoyl peroxide. Add a topical or oral antibiotic only with benzoyl peroxide so resistance is limited; combined oral contraceptives or spironolactone help selected women; isotretinoin is a major teratogen and needs a formal pregnancy-prevention program.

TRETINOIN.clue: Topical retinoid for comedonal acne that is applied at night and avoided in pregnancy
TRETINOIN.rationale: Tretinoin causes dryness and sun sensitivity and works over weeks, not days. It is not the systemic teratogen isotretinoin, but topical retinoids are still avoided in pregnancy; combine it with benzoyl peroxide at a separate time if irritation allows.

COMEDONE.clue: Blackhead or whitehead that defines acne and is absent in rosacea
COMEDONE.rationale: Comedones respond to topical retinoids. Closed comedones are whiteheads; open ones are black from oxidized pigment, not dirt; scrubbing does not remove them and worsens irritation.

CELLULITIS.clue: Spreading skin infection; nonpurulent disease is usually streptococcal and purulent disease raises concern for MRSA
CELLULITIS.rationale: Mark the border and elevate the limb. Cephalexin is a typical choice for nonpurulent cellulitis; an abscess needs drainage; if the border is ignored and the person is septic, or if crepitus or pain out of proportion appears, this is a deeper infection and an emergency.

ERYSIPELAS.clue: Superficial streptococcal skin infection with a sharply raised, bright red border
ERYSIPELAS.rationale: Erysipelas is more superficial and better demarcated than ordinary cellulitis. Penicillin or amoxicillin treats classic facial or leg disease; failure to improve, bullae, or systemic toxicity needs reassessment for a deeper or resistant infection.

ABSCESS.clue: Pus collection whose primary treatment is drainage, not an antibiotic alone
ABSCESS.rationale: Incision and drainage is the essential step for a fluctuant abscess. Add an MRSA-active antibiotic when there is cellulitis, fever, or immunosuppression; packing decisions depend on the cavity; a recurrent abscess in the axilla or groin may be hidradenitis.

MRSA.clue: Resistant staphylococcus that requires drainage of an abscess plus an active oral agent when antibiotics are used
MRSA.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, doxycycline, and clindamycin are common oral options when the local antibiogram agrees. Cephalexin does not cover MRSA; decolonization is considered for recurrences, not for a single drained boil.

IMPETIGO.clue: Honey-colored crusts from staph or strep; a later kidney complication can still occur after the skin is treated
IMPETIGO.rationale: Limited impetigo is treated with topical mupirocin. Numerous lesions need an oral agent such as cephalexin; post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis can follow skin infection, whereas rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis rather than impetigo.

MUPIROCIN.clue: Topical antibiotic for limited impetigo and for nasal decolonization in selected recurrent staph infections
MUPIROCIN.rationale: Mupirocin is not a substitute for drainage of an abscess or for oral therapy when impetigo is widespread. Resistance rises with indiscriminate use; it does not treat fungal skin infection.

HONEY.rationale: Honey-colored crusts on the face of a child are impetigo until proven otherwise. Bullous lesions are staphylococcal; treat the infection and watch urine if edema or dark urine appears later, because glomerulonephritis is still possible.

TINEA.clue: Dermatophyte infection; scalp disease needs an oral antifungal, and nystatin does not work
TINEA.rationale: Tinea corporis and pedis respond to topical terbinafine or an azole. Tinea capitis needs oral therapy, often terbinafine or griseofulvin, plus treatment of household sources; a potassium hydroxide prep confirms the diagnosis before months of oral nail therapy.

TERBINAFINE.clue: Oral antifungal for confirmed nail dermatophyte infection; check the liver history before a long course
TERBINAFINE.rationale: Do not start oral terbinafine on the appearance of a thick nail alone, because many dystrophic nails are not fungal. It does not treat Candida nails as its main role; baseline liver disease is a reason to choose another plan; topical nail lacquers rarely cure matrix disease.

NYSTATIN.clue: Antifungal that treats mucosal yeast but not skin ringworm
NYSTATIN.rationale: Nystatin suspension treats oral thrush, and the cream treats Candida in skin folds. Dermatophyte infections need an azole or terbinafine; swish-and-swallow is used when esophageal disease is not the concern; odynophagia needs a different evaluation.

KERION.clue: Boggy inflammatory scalp reaction to tinea capitis that can scar and still needs an oral antifungal
KERION.rationale: A kerion is often mistaken for a bacterial abscess. Incision does not cure it; oral antifungal therapy is required, and a bacterial superinfection is treated only when truly present; hair loss can be permanent if treatment is delayed.

SCABIES.clue: Highly itchy mite infestation of finger webs and wrists; treat close contacts and expect itch to outlast the mites
SCABIES.rationale: Permethrin from the neck down, repeated in a week, is standard treatment, with oral ivermectin for outbreaks or crusted disease. Wash fomites; the rash can persist for weeks after the mites are dead, so do not stack steroid after steroid without retreating if new burrows appear.

PERMETHRIN.clue: Topical agent for scabies and for head lice
PERMETHRIN.rationale: For scabies, apply permethrin to the whole skin below the neck, including under nails, and repeat as directed. For lice, resistance exists, so failure means a different agent rather than endless repeats of the same one; it is not for bacterial impetigo.

IVERMECTIN.clue: Oral antiparasitic used for crusted scabies, outbreaks, and some resistant lice
IVERMECTIN.rationale: Ivermectin is dosed by weight and often repeated for scabies because it does not kill every egg. It is not first-line for ordinary limited scabies when permethrin can be applied correctly; do not confuse the human dose with veterinary products.

BURROW.clue: Thin track in the skin that is the classic lesion of scabies
BURROW.rationale: Burrows are sought in finger webs, wrists, and the waist. Excoriations can hide them; a mineral-oil scrape from a burrow shows the mite, eggs, or feces; treat household contacts even if they are not yet itchy.

PRURITUS.clue: Itch; nocturnal generalized itch with burrows is scabies, while itch without a primary rash may be systemic
PRURITUS.rationale: Cholestasis, lymphoma, kidney failure, and thyroid disease cause itch with few skin findings. Antihistamines help urticaria more than the itch of cholestasis or atopic dermatitis; find a primary lesion before calling itch psychogenic.

URTICARIA.clue: Transient itchy wheals that move from place to place; airway symptoms make it anaphylaxis
URTICARIA.rationale: Ordinary urticaria is treated with a second-generation antihistamine, sometimes at a higher guideline dose. New wheals with hypotension, vomiting, or wheeze need epinephrine, not diphenhydramine first; chronic urticaria lasting beyond six weeks needs a broader look.

ANAPHYLAXIS.clue: IgE-mediated emergency of airway, breathing, or circulation; intramuscular epinephrine is the first drug
ANAPHYLAXIS.rationale: Inject epinephrine into the mid-outer thigh and repeat if needed. Antihistamines and steroids do not replace it; observe for a biphasic reaction; a vaccine or drug that caused anaphylaxis is contraindicated later; a mild local reaction is not.

EPINEPHRINE.clue: First drug for anaphylaxis, given intramuscularly in the mid-outer thigh, and also nebulized for severe croup
EPINEPHRINE.rationale: The anaphylaxis dose is given immediately and may be repeated. Prescribe an autoinjector and an action plan after an episode; in croup, nebulized epinephrine is for significant stridor and the child is observed afterward; it is not the treatment of ordinary urticaria.

ANGIOEDEMA.clue: Deep swelling of lips, tongue, or bowel that can be allergic or caused by an ACE inhibitor
ANGIOEDEMA.rationale: ACE-inhibitor angioedema can occur after years of use and is not IgE mediated, so antihistamines may fail. Stop the ACE inhibitor permanently; hereditary angioedema does not respond to epinephrine as its specific therapy and needs a specialist plan; airway swelling is an emergency either way.

NIKOLSKY.clue: Shearing of skin with gentle pressure, seen in toxic epidermal necrolysis and pemphigus
NIKOLSKY.rationale: A positive Nikolsky sign with mucosal involvement and a new drug suggests Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Stop the culprit drug, often an anticonvulsant, allopurinol, a sulfa, or certain antibiotics; this is burn-unit care, not a topical steroid visit.

MELANOMA.clue: Pigmented skin cancer recognized by asymmetry, an irregular border, color change, and evolution
MELANOMA.rationale: Evolution over time is the most useful warning. A changing mole needs a full-thickness biopsy, not a superficial shave that cannot measure depth; the ugly-duckling lesion that looks different from the person's other moles deserves attention even if it is small.

ABCDE.clue: Asymmetry, border, color, diameter, and evolution, the checklist for a suspicious mole
ABCDE.rationale: Evolution, meaning change in size, shape, or symptoms, matters more than a rigid size cutoff. Use the checklist to decide who needs biopsy, not to reassure a changing lesion that happens to be small; nodular melanoma can grow vertically with fewer classic features.

BASAL.clue: Most common skin cancer, often a pearly papule with telangiectasia and a rolled border
BASAL.rationale: Basal cell carcinoma grows locally and rarely metastasizes, but it still destroys tissue if ignored. Sun-exposed face and ears are typical sites; refer for destruction or excision rather than watching a nonhealing pearly sore.

SQUAMOUS.clue: Scaly or ulcerated skin cancer of sun-damaged skin that can arise in an actinic keratosis and can metastasize
SQUAMOUS.rationale: Squamous cell carcinoma is more likely than basal cell carcinoma to spread, especially on the lip, ear, or in immunosuppression. A horn or a nonhealing ulcer on sun-exposed skin needs biopsy; actinic keratoses are the precursor lesions treated before they progress.

KERATOSIS.clue: Sandpaper precancer on sun-exposed skin that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma
KERATOSIS.rationale: Actinic keratosis is treated with cryotherapy or a field treatment when many lesions are present. A thickened, tender, or rapidly growing lesion may already be invasive and needs a biopsy rather than another freeze; sun protection is the prevention.

BIOPSY.clue: Tissue sample required for a suspected melanoma or a nonhealing skin ulcer, not a visual guess
BIOPSY.rationale: Suspected melanoma is biopsied with a method that preserves depth. A shave that transects the base can wreck staging; most benign-appearing lesions do not need removal, but change, bleeding, or a nonhealing sore overrides a reassuring first impression.

SUNSCREEN.clue: Ultraviolet protection that reduces sunburn and skin-cancer risk when it is broad spectrum and actually applied
SUNSCREEN.rationale: Sunscreen is one part of protection, with clothing and shade. People on doxycycline, tetracyclines, or thiazides burn more easily; it does not treat an existing cancer; reapply after swimming rather than relying on a morning layer.

NEVUS.clue: Mole; one that looks different from the others or is changing needs a biopsy decision
NEVUS.rationale: A stable, symmetric brown nevus can be observed. Congenital large nevi and dysplastic-appearing moles need a different threshold; teach the ugly-duckling rule rather than promising that every dark lesion is safe.

KELOID.clue: Scar that grows beyond the original wound, more common in darker skin and on the chest and earlobes
KELOID.rationale: Keloids recur after simple excision, so prevention and steroid injection are preferred when possible. Do not confuse a keloid with a hypertrophic scar that stays within the wound; ear piercing is a common trigger.

LICHEN.clue: Purple, polygonal, pruritic papules, often with fine white lines, that can also affect the mouth
LICHEN.rationale: Lichen planus shows Wickham striae. Drugs and hepatitis C are associations worth asking about; oral erosions hurt and need exam so they are not dismissed as thrush; topical steroids are first-line for limited disease.

WICKHAM.clue: Fine white lines on the surface of lichen planus papules
WICKHAM.rationale: Wickham striae help separate lichen planus from psoriasis and eczema. Look in the mouth as well; if the lines are a lacy white patch that does not scrape off, also consider lichenoid drug eruption and, on the mucosa, leukoplakia that needs a different plan.

PETECHIAE.clue: Nonblanching pinpoint spots that, with fever, are meningococcemia until proven otherwise
PETECHIAE.rationale: Petechiae do not blanch the way a viral exanthem's erythema does. A well child with a few petechiae from coughing is different from a toxic child; new petechiae plus fever or headache need emergency antibiotics, not a next-day visit; platelets can be normal in meningococcal disease.

PURPURA.clue: Palpable purple lesions from vasculitis or from low platelets; the palpable form suggests vessel inflammation
PURPURA.rationale: Henoch-Schonlein purpura, now IgA vasculitis, shows palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks with joint and abdominal pain, and the kidneys must be followed. Meningococcemia is the lethal look-alike and the child is toxic; nonpalpable purpura suggests thrombocytopenia.

HENOCH.clue: Name linked to IgA vasculitis of childhood, with palpable purpura, joint pain, and abdominal pain
HENOCH.rationale: Check a urinalysis and kidney function because nephritis can appear later. Platelets are normal, which separates this from immune thrombocytopenia; severe abdominal pain can mean intussusception; most cases are supportive, but renal involvement changes follow-up.

SEQUELA.clue: Lasting complication, such as rheumatic heart disease after untreated strep throat or glomerulonephritis after strep skin infection
SEQUELA.rationale: A sequela is not the same as the acute infection. Antibiotics prevent rheumatic fever when strep throat is treated, but they do not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis once the immune response has started; teaching this distinction avoids false reassurance.

RHEUMATIC.clue: Inflammatory illness after strep throat that can scar heart valves; penicillin prevents it
RHEUMATIC.rationale: Acute rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis, not impetigo. Jones criteria combine carditis, arthritis, chorea, skin findings, and evidence of preceding strep; after an episode, long-term penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrence; joint pain that migrates is a clue.

PSGN.clue: Kidney complication after strep throat or skin infection, with dark urine and low complement
PSGN.rationale: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is supportive care plus treatment of any ongoing infection. Antibiotics do not reverse the immune injury; cola-colored urine, edema, and hypertension a week or two after strep are the picture; complement is low, unlike typical IgA nephropathy.

IGA.clue: Nephropathy with gross hematuria during a respiratory infection and a normal complement level
IGA.rationale: IgA nephropathy bleeds at the time of the infection, whereas post-strep glomerulonephritis follows one to two weeks later and lowers complement. IgA vasculitis is the systemic form with palpable purpura; persistent protein or reduced filtration needs nephrology.

NEISSERIA.clue: Gram-negative diplococcus that causes meningitis and a rapidly progressive petechial illness
NEISSERIA.rationale: Neisseria meningitidis is a droplet-precaution emergency. Do not delay antibiotics for a lumbar puncture if the person is unstable; close contacts need prophylaxis; the adolescent vaccine does not remove the need to recognize the septic picture.

MENINGITIS.clue: Infection of the meninges with fever, headache, and neck stiffness; do not delay antibiotics for a stable workup if the person is toxic
MENINGITIS.rationale: Kernig and Brudzinski signs support the diagnosis but their absence does not exclude it. Start droplets precautions for suspected bacterial disease; Listeria coverage is added in older adults, pregnant people, and immunocompromised patients; vaccination prevents many meningococcal and pneumococcal cases.

KERNIG.clue: Pain on extending the knee with the hip flexed, a sign of meningeal irritation
KERNIG.rationale: Kernig sign is used with neck stiffness and Brudzinski sign, in which the hips flex when the neck is flexed. A negative sign does not rule out meningitis; fever plus a stiff neck is enough to send the person for emergency care.

NUCHAL.clue: Neck stiffness of meningitis, different from a sore trapezius
NUCHAL.rationale: Nuchal rigidity is resistance to passive flexion. Photophobia and headache strengthen the concern; a child who will not flex the neck and looks toxic needs emergency care even if a classic sign is hard to elicit.

SEPSIS.clue: Life-threatening organ dysfunction from infection; fever plus low blood pressure or confusion is not a routine office visit
SEPSIS.rationale: Sepsis needs immediate fluids, cultures, and antibiotics in an emergency setting. A lactate and source search happen there; primary care's role is to recognize the toxic patient, including the older adult who is afebrile but acutely confused.

FEVER.clue: Elevated temperature that in a neonate is a full sepsis evaluation until serious infection is excluded
FEVER.rationale: Fever in the first weeks of life is not managed with advice to push fluids. Older infants are risk-stratified, but a toxic appearance overrides any reassuring score; antipyretics treat comfort; they do not tell you the cause.

NEONATE.clue: Infant in the first weeks of life, in whom fever, poor feeding, or jaundice on day one is urgent
NEONATE.rationale: Neonates have few specific signs. Lethargy, temperature instability, or a bulging fontanel can be sepsis or meningitis; do not attribute early jaundice to feeding alone; vitamin K, eye prophylaxis, hepatitis B vaccine, and the metabolic screen are newborn standards.

DEHYDRATION.clue: Fluid deficit shown by dry mucosa, no tears, delayed capillary refill, and fewer wet diapers
DEHYDRATION.rationale: Mild dehydration from gastroenteritis is treated with small, frequent oral rehydration. Severe lethargy, shock, or inability to keep fluids down needs intravenous fluid; antimotility drugs are not for young children with acute gastroenteritis.

OLIGURIA.clue: Low urine output that signals dehydration, shock, or acute kidney injury
OLIGURIA.rationale: Ask about wet diapers and weigh infants rather than guessing from thirst. Oliguria with a full bladder is obstruction, not dehydration; in sepsis, low urine output means perfusion is failing.

TURGOR.clue: Skin elasticity that is poor in dehydration, tested over the abdomen in an infant
TURGOR.rationale: Tenting supports significant volume loss but is a late sign. Mucosa, tears, capillary refill, and urine output change earlier; older skin tents even when hydration is normal, so do not use turgor alone in geriatrics.

FONTANEL.clue: Soft spot that is sunken in dehydration and bulging, when the infant is calm, in raised intracranial pressure
FONTANEL.rationale: The anterior fontanel usually closes during the second year. A bulging fontanel with fever is meningitis until proven otherwise; crying temporarily bulges it, so examine the infant at rest; a sunken fontanel supports dehydration but is not the only sign.

PYLORIC.clue: Infant gastric-outlet narrowing with projectile nonbilious vomiting and an olive-shaped mass
PYLORIC.rationale: Pyloric stenosis presents in the first weeks to months, more often in boys. The metabolic picture is hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; ultrasound confirms it, and the treatment is surgery after fluids are corrected; bilious vomiting is a different emergency.

OLIVE.clue: Palpable mass of pyloric stenosis, felt in the right upper abdomen of a hungry infant
OLIVE.rationale: The olive is not always felt, so a classic vomiting history still needs ultrasound. Do not diagnose ordinary reflux when vomiting is projectile and the infant is failing to gain; electrolytes are corrected before pyloromyotomy.

ALKALOSIS.clue: High pH; the hypochloremic hypokalemic form accompanies prolonged vomiting from pyloric stenosis
ALKALOSIS.rationale: Gastric fluid loss removes acid and chloride. Respiratory alkalosis is a different problem, seen with hyperventilation and early salicylate poisoning; do not give an antiemetic and discharge a young infant with projectile vomiting.

CURRANT.clue: Jelly-like bloody stool that is a late sign of intussusception
CURRANT.rationale: Currant-jelly stool means mucosal ischemia has already occurred. Earlier intussusception is intermittent colicky pain, drawing up the legs, and a sausage-shaped mass; ultrasound shows a target sign, and an air enema is often both diagnostic and curative.

SAUSAGE.rationale: A sausage-shaped mass in a toddler with episodic pain is intussusception. Lethargy can be the dominant sign, so do not require jelly stool; an air or contrast enema reduces many cases; perforation or peritonitis needs surgery instead.

ENEMA.clue: Air or contrast study that both diagnoses and often reduces intussusception
ENEMA.rationale: The enema is performed where surgery is available in case of perforation. It is not a home treatment; bloody stool and shock are late; any toddler with intermittent severe pain needs this diagnosis considered.

TARGET.clue: Ultrasound appearance of intussusception, and also the bull's-eye rash of early Lyme disease
TARGET.rationale: A target sign on abdominal ultrasound supports intussusception. Erythema migrans is the expanding target rash of Lyme disease and is diagnosed clinically in an endemic area; serology can be negative early; context tells these apart.

MECONIUM.clue: First sticky stool; failure to pass it suggests Hirschsprung disease or cystic fibrosis
MECONIUM.rationale: Most term infants pass meconium within the first day or two. Delayed passage with a tight empty rectum suggests Hirschsprung disease, unlike functional constipation where the rectal vault is full; meconium ileus is a cystic fibrosis presentation.

KERNICTERUS.clue: Brain injury from extreme newborn bilirubin, prevented by recognizing jaundice that appears too early or rises too fast
KERNICTERUS.rationale: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathologic. Lethargy, poor feeding, and a high-pitched cry are late neurologic warnings; phototherapy thresholds depend on age in hours and risk, so use the current chart rather than a single number; hemolysis and poor intake are common drivers.

MILIA.clue: Tiny white keratin cysts on a newborn face that resolve without squeezing
MILIA.rationale: Milia are benign and are not neonatal acne or infection. Parents should not scrub them; erythema toxicum is the other common benign newborn rash, with migratory red patches and eosinophil-filled pustules.

APGAR.clue: One- and five-minute newborn score of color, pulse, reflex, tone, and breathing that guides resuscitation, not long-term intelligence
APGAR.rationale: APGAR is appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, and respiration. A low score prompts support; it does not predict school performance; do not delay ventilation to finish the score; the five-minute score reflects response to resuscitation.

ORTOLANI.clue: Hip maneuver that reduces a dislocated hip by abduction and a lifting motion
ORTOLANI.rationale: Ortolani produces a clunk of entry as a dislocated hip reduces. It is not the same as Barlow, which tries to dislocate an unstable hip; a positive exam, breech history, or a click that is actually a clunk needs imaging and referral; most benign clicks are not dysplasia.

BARLOW.clue: Hip maneuver that tries to dislocate an unstable hip with adduction and posterior pressure
BARLOW.rationale: Barlow is the provocative test; Ortolani is the reducing test. Do them gently, one hip at a time; risk is higher after breech presentation and in girls with a family history; ultrasound is used in young infants because the femoral head is not yet ossified.

BREECH.clue: Fetal buttocks-first position that raises the risk of developmental hip dysplasia
BREECH.rationale: Breech presentation is a reason for a careful hip exam and a low threshold for ultrasound. It also affects delivery planning; do not equate a breech history with dysplasia if the exam and imaging are normal, but do not skip the evaluation.

HEEL.clue: Part of the foot used for the newborn metabolic blood spot
HEEL.rationale: The heel stick screens for conditions such as phenylketonuria and congenital hypothyroidism. A specimen drawn too early or poorly can be falsely reassuring, so follow the state protocol for timing and repeats; an abnormal result is confirmed, not ignored.

PKU.clue: Metabolic disease on the newborn screen in which phenylalanine cannot be processed and a special diet prevents intellectual disability
PKU.rationale: Phenylketonuria must be treated before symptoms appear, which is why screening exists. A positive screen is confirmed with quantitative testing; mothers with PKU also need strict control in pregnancy to protect the fetus.

HEARING.clue: Newborn sense that is screened before discharge; a failed screen needs follow-up, not reassurance
HEARING.rationale: Otoacoustic emissions or auditory brainstem response can be affected by fluid or noise. A failed inpatient screen is repeated and referred if it fails again; later speech delay should trigger a hearing test even if the newborn screen was normal.

CYANOTIC.clue: Blue from right-to-left shunting; a newborn saturation screen looks for critical congenital heart disease
CYANOTIC.rationale: Failing the pulse-oximetry screen needs evaluation before discharge, not a promise that the hands are just cold. Persistent cyanosis, a murmur, or poor feeding also needs a cardiac look; hyperoxia testing and echocardiography are specialist tools.

WALKING.clue: Gross-motor skill expected around the first birthday; not doing it by the middle of the second year needs evaluation
WALKING.rationale: Most children walk near 12 months, and the range is wide. Failure to walk independently by 18 months is a red flag, as is a loss of a previously gained skill; check tone, hips, and whether the child was late on earlier milestones.

BABBLE.clue: Repetitive consonant sounds expected in the middle of the first year
BABBLE.rationale: Babbling usually appears around six months. Absence of babbling by the later part of the first year, especially with poor response to name, needs a hearing test and a developmental referral; do not wait for a missed skill to return on its own.

SMILE.clue: Social response expected by about two months of age
SMILE.rationale: A social smile is a developmental milestone, not gas. No social smile by about two to three months needs evaluation of vision, bonding, and neurologic development; it is separate from the reflex facial movement of a newborn.

PINCER.clue: Thumb-and-finger grasp that appears near the end of the first year
PINCER.rationale: A pincer grasp lets an infant pick up small food and is also a choking-risk moment. Absence well after the first birthday, with other fine-motor delays, needs evaluation; it follows a raking grasp rather than appearing first.

STRANGER.clue: Anxiety toward unfamiliar people that appears in the second half of the first year and is a normal social milestone
STRANGER.rationale: Stranger anxiety shows the infant distinguishes caregivers. Its total absence, with no joint attention or response to name, is more concerning than its presence; it is not a reason to force separation without comfort.

AUTISM.clue: Neurodevelopmental condition suggested by poor joint attention, no response to name, and loss of language or social skills
AUTISM.rationale: Any regression of skills needs prompt evaluation rather than watchful waiting. Screening tools such as the modified checklist are used at recommended well visits, but a parental concern is enough to refer; early intervention does not require waiting for a specialty label.

REGRESSION.clue: Loss of skills already gained, a red flag for autism, a neurodegenerative disease, or a seizure disorder
REGRESSION.rationale: Regression is never a normal variant. Document what was lost and when; hearing loss can look like language regression; refer rather than offering reassurance that children develop at their own pace.

MILESTONE.clue: Developmental achievement; losing one, or missing several in a domain, needs referral rather than more waiting
MILESTONE.rationale: Know the major motor, language, and social milestones well enough to recognize delay. Correct for prematurity in the early years; a single borderline skill with an otherwise typical exam can be rechecked soon; global delay cannot.

HEADSS.clue: Adolescent interview covering home, education, activities, drugs, sexuality, and safety or mood
HEADSS.rationale: HEADSS is done with the adolescent alone for part of the visit. Confidentiality has legal limits when someone is in danger; substance use, depression, and sexual health are asked directly; the parent history does not replace this conversation.

TANNER.clue: Scale that describes pubertal development of breasts, genitals, and pubic hair
TANNER.rationale: Tanner staging is an exam finding, not a lab. Delayed or very early puberty is judged against the stage and the tempo, not against one photograph; precocious puberty thresholds have shifted, so refer when development is clearly early rather than quoting a single disputed age.

SCOLIOSIS.clue: Lateral spinal curve screened with a forward-bend test during adolescent growth
SCOLIOSIS.rationale: The Adams forward-bend test shows a rib hump. Significant curves are referred for measurement and a decision about bracing or surgery; painful scoliosis is not the typical idiopathic pattern and needs imaging for another cause.

ADAMS.clue: Forward-bend test for a rib hump in scoliosis
ADAMS.rationale: Adams test is done with the back bare and the examiner behind the patient. A hump suggests rotation, not just poor posture; it does not replace radiography when the exam is clearly abnormal or when pain or neurologic signs are present.

CONCUSSION.clue: Traumatic brain dysfunction managed with a brief period of relative rest and a graduated return, never same-day return to play
CONCUSSION.rationale: Red flags are worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, weakness, or declining alertness. Cognitive and physical activity increase in steps; a second impact before recovery is dangerous; school accommodations matter as much as sport clearance.

AOM.clue: Middle-ear infection diagnosed by a bulging, immobile eardrum plus acute symptoms, not by a red drum alone
AOM.rationale: Amoxicillin is first-line when antibiotics are indicated and the child has not recently failed it. Pain control is mandatory; some older children with mild unilateral disease can be observed; a red drum without effusion is not acute otitis media.

BULGING.clue: Eardrum finding that, with middle-ear effusion and acute symptoms, defines acute otitis media
BULGING.rationale: Bulging reflects pressure from pus. Mild redness alone does not; if the drum perforates and drains, pain often improves suddenly; recurrent infections with hearing loss are a reason to discuss tubes, not endless antibiotics.

EFFUSION.clue: Fluid behind the eardrum without acute infection; antibiotics are not routine
EFFUSION.rationale: Otitis media with effusion can follow a cold and may muffle hearing. Watch most cases; persistent effusion with hearing loss or speech delay needs audiology and possible referral; it is not treated like acute otitis media.

OTALGIA.clue: Ear pain from otitis media, otitis externa, dental disease, or throat disease
OTALGIA.rationale: Tugging the pinna or pressing the tragus points to the canal, not the middle ear. Dental and temporomandibular pain refer to the ear with a normal drum; in a sick child, ear pain plus a bulging drum is middle-ear infection.

OTITIS.clue: Ear infection; externa hurts when the ear is moved, while media is a problem behind an intact or bulging drum
OTITIS.rationale: Otitis externa is treated with topical antibiotic drops and a wick if the canal is swollen. Keep the ear dry; diabetes with severe ear pain and granulation tissue is malignant external otitis, an osteomyelitis emergency, not a routine drop.

TRAGUS.clue: Cartilage in front of the canal; tenderness here suggests swimmer's ear rather than middle-ear infection
TRAGUS.rationale: Tragal or pinna tenderness plus canal swelling is otitis externa. The middle-ear drum may not even be visible; topical therapy reaches the infection only if a wick is placed when the canal is closed by swelling.

CERUMEN.clue: Earwax that can cause hearing loss and that is removed when it blocks the drum, not routinely
CERUMEN.rationale: Softening drops and irrigation are used only when the drum is known to be intact. Do not irrigate a perforated drum or a canal after ear surgery; impacted wax is a common reason for a failed hearing or tinnitus complaint.

WEBER.clue: Tuning-fork test that lateralizes to the bad ear in conductive loss and to the good ear in sensorineural loss
WEBER.rationale: Weber is interpreted with Rinne. If sound is louder in the affected ear, think obstruction or otosclerosis; if it is louder in the better ear, think sensorineural loss on the quiet side; neither test replaces audiometry.

RINNE.clue: Tuning-fork test in which bone conduction louder than air conduction means conductive hearing loss
RINNE.rationale: A normal, or positive, Rinne has air louder than bone. A negative Rinne, bone louder than air, is conductive loss; do it on both ears and combine it with Weber; sudden sensorineural loss is an urgent referral, not wax, until proven otherwise.

CONDUCTIVE.clue: Hearing loss from wax, fluid, or ossicles, in which the Weber test goes toward the affected ear
CONDUCTIVE.rationale: Conductive loss is often correctable. Sensorineural loss is cochlear or neural and Weber lateralizes away from it; sudden sensorineural loss is treated as urgent; a child with conductive loss from chronic effusion needs a hearing check before speech delay is blamed on behavior.

PRESBYCUSIS.clue: Age-related high-frequency hearing loss that makes speech hard to follow in noise
PRESBYCUSIS.rationale: Presbycusis is sensorineural and bilateral. Sudden one-sided loss is not presbycusis and needs urgent evaluation; hearing aids help when the person will use them; screen older adults who withdraw from conversation rather than waiting for a complaint.

TINNITUS.clue: Ringing in the ear from noise, Meniere disease, aspirin, a loop diuretic, or an aminoglycoside
TINNITUS.rationale: Unilateral tinnitus with hearing loss needs imaging consideration for a vestibular schwannoma. Pulsatile tinnitus needs a vascular evaluation; bilateral high-frequency tinnitus fits noise exposure or presbycusis; stopping the offending drug matters when a medicine is the cause.

VERTIGO.clue: Spinning sensation; brief episodes with position change suggest a benign positional cause, not a stroke, unless red flags are present
VERTIGO.rationale: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is confirmed with Dix-Hallpike and treated with a canalith repositioning maneuver. Hearing loss and tinnitus suggest Meniere disease; continuous vertigo after a virus suggests vestibular neuritis; sudden vertigo with other neurologic signs is a posterior circulation stroke.

EPLEY.clue: Canalith repositioning maneuver that treats posterior-canal benign positional vertigo
EPLEY.rationale: Epley is done after Dix-Hallpike confirms the affected posterior canal. It is not the treatment of Meniere disease or of a cerebellar stroke; warn that symptoms may recur and that a second maneuver is often needed.

HALLPIKE.clue: Positional test that brings on torsional nystagmus in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
HALLPIKE.rationale: Dix-Hallpike is done with the head turned and the person laid back quickly. The nystagmus is delayed and fatigues; immediate vertical nystagmus or other neurologic signs are not typical benign positional vertigo and need imaging.

MENIERE.clue: Inner-ear disease of fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness, and longer attacks of vertigo
MENIERE.rationale: Meniere disease is not a 20-second positional spin. Salt restriction and a diuretic are often tried, and sudden permanent hearing loss needs ENT care; acoustic neuroma is the serious mimic when hearing loss and tinnitus are unilateral and progressive.

NYSTAGMUS.clue: Involuntary eye jerking; a few beats at the far end of gaze can be normal
NYSTAGMUS.rationale: Direction-changing or vertical nystagmus is central until proven otherwise. Peripheral vestibular nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixing the gaze; describe the direction rather than only writing that nystagmus is present.

OTOSCOPE.clue: Instrument used to see the eardrum and the canal; a pneumatic bulb tests drum mobility
OTOSCOPE.rationale: Brace your hand on the face so a sudden move does not injure the canal. Pull the pinna to straighten the canal; a red drum without landmarks or mobility problems is not enough to diagnose acute otitis media.

GLAUCOMA.clue: Optic neuropathy; the acute angle-closure form is a painful red eye with halos, a mid-dilated pupil, and nausea
GLAUCOMA.rationale: Acute angle closure is an eye emergency. Do not dilate the pupil; chronic open-angle glaucoma is silent and found by pressure, disc, and field testing; a headache plus a red eye and a cloudy cornea is not migraine.

HALOS.clue: Rings around lights seen in acute angle-closure glaucoma and sometimes in cataracts
HALOS.rationale: Halos with severe eye pain, a mid-dilated pupil, and nausea are angle closure. Halos with gradual glare and a preserved pupil are more often cataract; the painful red eye is referred the same day.

PUPIL.clue: Opening that is mid-dilated and poorly reactive in acute angle-closure glaucoma
PUPIL.rationale: A fixed mid-dilated pupil with a red painful eye is a pressure emergency. An afferent pupillary defect means optic-nerve or severe retinal disease; pinpoint pupils suggest opioids or a pontine lesion; asymmetry with ptosis and anhidrosis is Horner syndrome.

CATARACT.clue: Lens opacity causing gradual glare and reduced acuity, the leading reversible cause of vision loss in older adults
CATARACT.rationale: Cataract surgery is considered when function is limited, not at a fixed acuity alone. A red reflex that is absent or asymmetric needs explanation; sudden vision loss is not a cataract and is an emergency.

PRESBYOPIA.clue: Age-related loss of near focus as the lens stiffens
PRESBYOPIA.rationale: Presbyopia is corrected with reading lenses and is not a disease of the retina. It begins in midlife; sudden near-vision change, distortion, or a curtain over the vision is not presbyopia.

MACULAR.clue: Central retinal area whose degeneration causes loss of central vision and distorted lines on a grid
MACULAR.rationale: Dry macular degeneration is monitored and supported with the indicated vitamin formulation in selected intermediate disease. Wet disease, with sudden distortion or a bleed, needs urgent retinal treatment; an Amsler grid finds change between visits.

AMSLER.clue: Grid used at home to detect new distortion from macular disease
AMSLER.rationale: A new bend in the lines is a reason for prompt retinal evaluation, especially if wet degeneration is a concern. The grid does not replace dilated exams; teach the person to check one eye at a time.

DRUSEN.clue: Yellow deposits under the retina that mark age-related macular degeneration
DRUSEN.rationale: Drusen are seen on the fundus exam. They are not diabetic exudates, which sit in a different pattern with microaneurysms; many small drusen are followed; conversion to wet disease presents as sudden metamorphopsia.

HORDEOLUM.clue: Acute painful stye of an eyelid gland, treated with warm compresses
HORDEOLUM.rationale: A hordeolum is infectious and points to a lash or internal gland. A chalazion is the chronic sterile granuloma that may follow and is less tender; vision change, fever, or spreading redness of the lid is more than a stye.

CONJUNCTIVA.clue: Membrane that is purulent in bacterial pink eye, watery in viral disease, and itchy in allergy
CONJUNCTIVA.rationale: Bacterial conjunctivitis has thick discharge that reaccumulates. Viral disease often has a preauricular node and is contagious; allergic disease itches and is bilateral; pain, photophobia, or a corneal stain suggests keratitis, not simple pink eye.

ITCHY.clue: Sensation that points to allergic conjunctivitis or to atopic and scabetic skin disease
ITCHY.rationale: Itchy eyes with watery discharge and cobblestoning are allergic. Pain and light sensitivity are not; on the skin, itch without a burrow still needs a look for scabies when it is nocturnal and household members are affected.

NOSEBLEED.clue: Anterior bleeding managed by leaning forward and pinching the soft nose for a sustained time
NOSEBLEED.rationale: Most nosebleeds stop with correct pressure, not with packing the vestibule with tissue and peeking. Recurrent bleeding on an anticoagulant, or bleeding from the posterior nose, needs more than home pressure; moisturize afterward and treat allergic rhinitis if it is the driver.

POLYP.clue: Grape-like nasal growth that, with asthma and aspirin sensitivity, forms Samter triad
POLYP.rationale: Nasal polyps cause obstruction and loss of smell. Intranasal corticosteroids are first-line; a child with polyps needs evaluation for cystic fibrosis; aspirin and NSAIDs can provoke bronchospasm in the aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease triad.

SAMTER.clue: Triad of asthma, nasal polyps, and aspirin or NSAID sensitivity
SAMTER.rationale: People with Samter triad should avoid aspirin and NSAIDs. A leukotriene modifier is sometimes used, with the neuropsychiatric warning of montelukast in mind; polyps plus late-onset asthma should prompt the question about aspirin reactions.

LORATADINE.clue: Second-generation antihistamine for allergic rhinitis and hives that is less sedating than older agents
LORATADINE.rationale: Loratadine helps sneeze and itch more than nasal congestion. An intranasal corticosteroid is more effective for congestion; first-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine are anticholinergic and are poor choices in older adults.

ALLERGIC.clue: Mechanism of seasonal rhinitis, of many conjunctivitides, and of true anaphylaxis to a drug or vaccine
ALLERGIC.rationale: Allergic rhinitis is itchy and sneezing, with pale turbinates. Infection is painful and purulent; a drug rash that is delayed and morbilliform is often not a true allergy, whereas hives, bronchospasm, and hypotension are; document the reaction precisely.

INHALER.clue: Device whose technique must be watched before asthma or COPD therapy is stepped up
INHALER.rationale: Common errors are not exhaling first, actuating too early, and not holding the breath. A spacer fixes coordination problems with a pressurized canister; dry-powder devices have different steps; adherence, not just the prescription, explains many uncontrolled patients.

THRUSH.clue: Oral candidiasis that appears as white plaques that scrape off, a complication of inhaled corticosteroids
THRUSH.rationale: Rinse and spit after an inhaled corticosteroid and use a spacer. Thrush scrapes off and leaves a red base, unlike leukoplakia; painful swallowing suggests esophageal candidiasis, which is more than a topical problem and is an HIV clue.

CRACKLES.clue: Discontinuous lung sounds of fluid or fibrosis; in heart failure they sit at the bases with edema and an extra heart sound
CRACKLES.rationale: Fine crackles of fibrosis do not clear with cough. Coarse crackles of secretions may; focal crackles with fever suggest pneumonia; clear lungs do not exclude heart failure if the story and natriuretic peptide fit.

RHONCHI.clue: Low rattling sounds from secretions in larger airways that may clear with cough
RHONCHI.rationale: Rhonchi are common in bronchitis and COPD. They are not the musical sound of wheeze and not the fine sound of fibrosis; if they are new with fever and hypoxia, think pneumonia rather than a simple cold.

EGOPHONY.clue: Change of a spoken E to an A over consolidated lung
EGOPHONY.rationale: Egophony, whispered pectoriloquy, and increased tactile fremitus support consolidation. Effusion does the opposite: dullness with decreased fremitus and no egophony; use them when the radiograph will be delayed, not as a substitute for imaging when the person is ill.

DULLNESS.clue: Percussion note over consolidation or pleural fluid
DULLNESS.rationale: Dullness with bronchial breath sounds suggests pneumonia. Dullness with absent breath sounds suggests effusion; hyperresonance suggests pneumothorax or emphysema; always compare sides.

FREMITUS.clue: Vibration of speech felt on the chest; it increases over consolidation and decreases over fluid or air in the pleural space
FREMITUS.rationale: Tactile fremitus is a comparative exam. Obstruction of a bronchus also decreases it; it will not be reliable in a soft voice or a thick chest wall, so interpret it with percussion and auscultation.

CLUBBING.clue: Bulbous fingertip change from chronic lung, heart, or gastrointestinal disease, not from an acute infection
CLUBBING.rationale: New clubbing needs a cause, including lung cancer, bronchiectasis, interstitial disease, and cyanotic heart disease. It is not a finding of uncomplicated COPD as often as people expect; hypertrophic osteoarthropathy adds bone pain.

CYANOSIS.clue: Blue color from unsaturated hemoglobin; a blue tongue is a late, serious sign
CYANOSIS.rationale: Central cyanosis of the tongue means significant hypoxemia. Peripheral cyanosis can be cold exposure; in a newborn, persistent cyanosis needs the congenital-heart and lung evaluation, not warming alone; do not wait for cyanosis to give oxygen to a hypoxic patient.

PLEURISY.clue: Sharp chest pain that worsens with a breath, from pleural inflammation, pneumonia, or a pulmonary embolism
PLEURISY.rationale: Pleuritic pain with sudden dyspnea is a clot until proven otherwise in the right-risk patient. Reproducible chest-wall tenderness suggests musculoskeletal pain but does not fully exclude embolism or pneumonia; a rub may be heard and then disappear as fluid accumulates.

SILENT.clue: Chest that has stopped wheezing because air is barely moving, a sign of impending respiratory failure
SILENT.rationale: A silent chest in asthma is a reason for emergency care, not a sign the attack resolved. Look at work of breathing, speech, and oxygen saturation; fatigue, drowsiness, and a rising carbon dioxide follow; do not send the person home on more albuterol alone.

FOREIGN.clue: Inhaled object that causes sudden cough and unilateral wheeze, especially in a toddler
FOREIGN.rationale: A choking episode followed by unilateral findings is an airway foreign body until bronchoscopy excludes it. Do not reassure because the child looks briefly better; complete obstruction is treated with age-appropriate choking maneuvers, not a blind finger sweep.

SEIZURE.clue: Abnormal electrical brain activity; protect the person, do not place objects in the mouth, and treat a first event as a diagnosis to explain
SEIZURE.rationale: Time the event and place the person on the side after the convulsion. Benzodiazepines stop a prolonged seizure; bupropion and alcohol withdrawal lower the threshold; a new seizure in late pregnancy with hypertension is eclampsia and is treated with magnesium.

EPILEPSY.clue: Tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures; medicine choice must account for pregnancy, interactions, and the specific seizure type
EPILEPSY.rationale: Valproate is avoided in pregnancy because of neural-tube defects and developmental harm. Levetiracetam is often chosen when pregnancy is possible, with specialist input; do not stop a drug abruptly; counsel about driving laws, which vary by state.

PHENYTOIN.clue: Narrow-index antiseizure drug that causes gum overgrowth and is teratogenic
PHENYTOIN.rationale: Phenytoin levels are tricky because protein binding changes the free fraction. Gingival hyperplasia, nystagmus, and ataxia are clues; it induces many enzymes and fails hormonal contraception; it is not a first choice when pregnancy is possible.

VALPROATE.clue: Mood stabilizer and antiseizure drug that is a major teratogen and can injure the liver and lower platelets
VALPROATE.rationale: Valproate causes neural-tube defects and is avoided in people who can become pregnant. It also causes weight gain and a polycystic-ovary picture; check liver enzymes and platelets; it is not the mood stabilizer of choice in pregnancy.

LAMOTRIGINE.clue: Antiseizure and bipolar-maintenance drug that must be titrated slowly because of serious rash
LAMOTRIGINE.rationale: Lamotrigine rash can be Stevens-Johnson syndrome, so a new rash means stop and evaluate. It does not treat acute mania; estrogen contraceptives can lower its level, and the titration is restarted if doses are missed for several days.

LITHIUM.clue: Mood stabilizer with a narrow index; dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and thiazides raise the level
LITHIUM.rationale: Lithium causes tremor, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and kidney disease over time. Check level, TSH, and creatinine; pregnancy exposure is linked to Ebstein anomaly, so this is a specialist decision; toxicity looks like worsening tremor, confusion, and vomiting.

BIPOLAR.clue: Mood disorder of mania and depression; an antidepressant alone can precipitate mania
BIPOLAR.rationale: Screen for bipolar disorder before starting an antidepressant for depression. Lithium, certain anticonvulsants, and some antipsychotics are mood stabilizers; sleep loss can trigger mania; suicide risk is high and is asked about directly.

MANIA.clue: Elevated or irritable mood with little sleep, grandiosity, and risky behavior that is not ordinary happiness
