Clean minor wounds need a booster after ten years; dirty or puncture wounds after five; immune globulin is added when the primary series was never completed and the wound is tetanus-prone; the disease causes spasms and autonomic instability and is not treated with antibiotic alone.

DIPHTHERIA.clue: Toxin-mediated throat infection with a membrane that can obstruct the airway, prevented by routine immunization
DIPHTHERIA.rationale: Diphtheria is now rare because of vaccination, but a gray pharyngeal membrane and neck swelling in an underimmunized person is the classic picture. Antitoxin and antibiotic are hospital care; the adult booster keeps immunity from drifting.

POLIO.clue: Enterovirus that can cause irreversible paralysis; inactivated vaccine is the form used in the United States
POLIO.rationale: Polio vaccination is part of the childhood series. Travelers to areas with circulating virus may need an additional adult dose under current guidance; acute flaccid weakness after a febrile illness is a public-health emergency, not a routine neurology referral next month.

ROTAVIRUS.clue: Infant diarrheal virus prevented by an oral live vaccine given only in early infancy
ROTAVIRUS.rationale: Rotavirus causes dehydrating gastroenteritis. The oral vaccine is live and is not started after the age window closes, because of intussusception risk; breastfeeding is not a reason to skip it; hospitalized infants and those with severe combined immunodeficiency have special precautions.

INACTIVATED.clue: Killed or subunit vaccines that cannot replicate and are the influenza and pertussis products used in pregnancy
INACTIVATED.rationale: Inactivated vaccines are acceptable in pregnancy and in most immunocompromised people. They may work less well when immunity is poor, but they do not cause the disease; live vaccines are the ones that are withheld; a mild illness is not a contraindication.

HIB.clue: Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine that prevents epiglottitis and invasive disease in infants
HIB.rationale: The Hib series is given in infancy. Unimmunized children remain at risk for epiglottitis; the vaccine does not cover nontypeable strains that still cause ear and sinus infections; a child with a completed series can still get other causes of a swollen epiglottis.

ACTIVITY.clue: Regular movement that lowers blood pressure, glucose, and depression risk and is the base of weight management
ACTIVITY.rationale: Prescribe activity the way you prescribe a drug: type, minutes, and how to start. It is first-line for osteoarthritis, fibromyalgia, and prevention of diabetes; chest pain or severe dyspnea with exertion is a reason to evaluate before pushing intensity; a walking program is treatment for claudication.

LIFESTYLE.clue: Diet, movement, sleep, tobacco, and alcohol changes that are first-line for blood pressure, glucose, and lipids
LIFESTYLE.rationale: Lifestyle therapy is not a delay tactic when a statin or a pressure medicine is clearly indicated, and it is not optional window dressing. Specific advice beats a vague instruction to be healthier; recheck the numbers rather than assuming the advice worked.

DASH.clue: Eating pattern rich in produce and low-fat dairy and lower in sodium that lowers blood pressure
DASH.rationale: The DASH pattern reduces blood pressure within weeks. Sodium restriction adds benefit; it is compatible with diabetes care; it does not replace medicine when the pressure is markedly high or when there is heart failure or kidney disease that needs a drug.

SOAP.clue: Four-part note built from the patient's story, the findings, the impression, and the treatment
SOAP.rationale: SOAP keeps a visit reproducible: subjective history, objective exam and tests, assessment, and plan. The assessment should name the diagnosis, not repeat the story; the plan includes medicines, education, and follow-up so another clinician can continue care.

SUBJECTIVE.clue: The history portion of a note, told in the patient's words and including the review of systems
SUBJECTIVE.rationale: Subjective data are what the person reports: pain, onset, medicines tried, and goals. Do not put your exam findings here; quote the chief concern; a good history narrows the differential before any test is ordered.

OBJECTIVE.clue: The note section that records vital signs, exam findings, and test results
OBJECTIVE.rationale: Objective data are observed or measured, not believed. Include pertinent negatives that change the diagnosis, such as a nonfocal neurologic exam or a soft abdomen; do not copy a prior exam forward without looking.

PLAN.clue: The note section that records treatment, education, return precautions, and follow-up
PLAN.rationale: A plan names the drug, the dose, what to do if symptoms worsen, and when to return. It includes referrals and the tests still pending; patient education is part of the plan, not an afterthought; safety-net advice is what makes outpatient care safe.

JOINT.clue: Structure that is hot, red, and exquisitely painful when bacteria invade it; that picture is an emergency
JOINT.rationale: A single hot joint is infection or crystal disease until proven otherwise. Aspirate before antibiotics when the person is stable enough, and never inject steroid into a joint that might be infected; gonorrhea is a classic cause in a younger adult; chronic many-joint disease is a different tempo.

INJURY.clue: Harm from a fall or trauma; in an older adult it triggers a review of medicines, vision, and home hazards
INJURY.rationale: One fall is a geriatric syndrome, not an accident to ignore. Look for orthostasis, sedatives, and footwear problems; a pressure injury is a different injury of immobility and is staged rather than described only as a red spot; nonaccidental injury in a child or older adult is reported.

INJECTION.clue: Progestin contraceptive given in the clinic every few months; fertility can take time to return
INJECTION.rationale: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is highly effective and often stops menses. It can reduce bone density with long use and cause weight gain; it is an option when estrogen is contraindicated and when daily adherence is unlikely; return of fertility is delayed compared with the implant.

GAD.clue: Excessive worry on more days than not for months, with restlessness, muscle tension, and poor sleep
GAD.rationale: Generalized anxiety disorder is treated with an SSRI or SNRI, buspirone, and cognitive behavioral therapy. Rule out hyperthyroidism, caffeine, and cardiopulmonary disease when the story is new; benzodiazepines are a short bridge, not maintenance, and are a poor choice in older adults.

VIOLENCE.clue: Harm by a partner or caregiver that is asked about in private and that has a safety plan, not a pamphlet only
VIOLENCE.rationale: Intimate-partner violence is associated with depression, unintended pregnancy, and injury. Ask when the person is alone; mandatory reporting rules for adults vary by state; child and vulnerable-adult abuse reporting does not; offer resources even when the person is not ready to leave.

ABUSE.clue: Nonaccidental harm to a child, older adult, or dependent person that clinicians are required to report
ABUSE.rationale: Injuries that do not match the history, delay in care, and patterned bruises are clues. Report suspected child abuse and elder abuse through the required channel; you do not need proof; document objectively; sexual abuse needs a specialized exam rather than an improvised one.

NEGLECT.clue: Failure to provide needed care, a form of elder and child maltreatment that is reported
NEGLECT.rationale: Neglect shows up as malnutrition, pressure injuries, missed medicines, and untreated conditions. It is as reportable as a bruise; caregiver overwhelm is a risk factor, not an excuse to skip the report; offer supports and still notify the agency.

MANDATED.clue: Legal duty of clinicians to report suspected child abuse and, in many settings, elder abuse
MANDATED.rationale: Mandated reporting does not require certainty. Document what you saw and what was said; tell the caregiver what you are required to do when it is safe to do so; failure to report is the error, not an imperfect report.

CONSENT.clue: Permission for care after the person understands the benefits, harms, and alternatives
CONSENT.rationale: Informed consent is a conversation, not a signature alone. Capacity is decision-specific; adolescents may consent to certain sexual-health and substance services under state law; a surrogate speaks when the person cannot, using the person's known goals.

AUTONOMY.clue: Ethical duty to respect an informed person's right to accept or refuse care
AUTONOMY.rationale: Autonomy does not require offering futile or harmful options, and it does not override the duty to protect a person who lacks capacity. Document the refusal and the safety-net plan; beneficence is the paired duty to act in the person's interest.

REFERRAL.clue: Transfer of part of care to a specialist when the problem exceeds primary-care scope or fails to improve
REFERRAL.rationale: A good referral states the question, the work already done, and the urgency. Do not send a surgical emergency to a routine clinic slot; keep responsibility for the whole person while the specialist handles one problem; close the loop on the result.

SCOPE.clue: Boundary of what a family nurse practitioner is trained and authorized to manage before referring
SCOPE.rationale: Scope includes primary care across the lifespan and excludes procedures and diseases you have not been trained to handle. State law and collaborative agreements further define it; staying inside scope is a patient-safety behavior, not a lack of confidence.

MCBURNEY.clue: Point of tenderness one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus in appendicitis
MCBURNEY.rationale: McBurney point tenderness supports appendicitis but is absent in retrocecal disease. Migration of pain from the umbilicus, anorexia, and fever complete the picture; imaging is used when the exam is unclear, especially in children and in pregnancy; do not give a laxative for undiagnosed right-lower pain.

ROVSING.clue: Right-lower pain when the left lower abdomen is pressed, a sign of peritoneal irritation from appendicitis
ROVSING.rationale: Rovsing sign is not required to refer a person with a classic migrating pain and fever. Rebound and guarding mean peritonitis; pregnancy shifts the appendix, so the classic point may be higher; a negative sign does not exclude the diagnosis.

PSOAS.clue: Hip-extension test that causes pain when an inflamed appendix lies on that muscle
PSOAS.rationale: The psoas sign supports a retrocecal appendix. Obturator pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip is the companion sign; neither replaces imaging or surgical judgment; hip disease itself can hurt with these movements, so use the whole story.

OBTURATOR.clue: Pain on internal rotation of the flexed hip that suggests a pelvic appendix
OBTURATOR.rationale: The obturator sign is one of several peritoneal signs in appendicitis. It is easy to forget and easy to overcall; combine it with migration of pain, fever, and white-cell count; gynecologic disease can produce the same pelvic pain.

REBOUND.clue: Pain when the examining hand is released, a sign of peritoneal inflammation
REBOUND.rationale: Rebound tenderness means the peritoneum is irritated, as in appendicitis, perforation, or pelvic inflammatory disease. It is unkind to elicit repeatedly; guarding that is involuntary is the related finding; a soft abdomen does not exclude early appendicitis.

GUARDING.rationale: Voluntary guarding relaxes when the person is distracted. Involuntary guarding does not; a rigid abdomen with fever is a surgical emergency; do not send the person home with an antispasmodic.

LYME.clue: Tickborne infection whose early rash is an expanding patch; doxycycline is usual treatment in nonpregnant adults
LYME.rationale: Erythema migrans is diagnosed clinically in an endemic area, and early serology is often negative. Later disease can cause facial palsy, heart block, or arthritis; prophylaxis after a tick bite is considered only when the tick, the time attached, and the geography all fit; amoxicillin is used when doxycycline cannot be.

MIGRANS.clue: Expanding red patch, often with central clearing, that is the rash of early Lyme disease
MIGRANS.rationale: Erythema migrans appears days to weeks after the tick bite and can be multiple if the infection has disseminated. Treat on sight in the right setting; it is not the petechial rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which needs doxycycline immediately and can involve palms and soles.

ROCKY.clue: Tickborne rickettsial illness with fever and a rash that starts on wrists and ankles; doxycycline is given at any age and should not wait for the rash
ROCKY.rationale: Rocky Mountain spotted fever kills when treatment is delayed for a laboratory result or because the patient is a child. The rash can be absent early; doxycycline is the drug in every age group; do not substitute a different antibiotic in a child.

TICK.clue: Vector of Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever; remove it promptly and completely
TICK.rationale: The longer a tick is attached, the higher the Lyme risk, but most bites do not transmit disease. Save the tick if identification would change prophylaxis; watch for fever or an expanding rash; do not use petroleum jelly or a burned match to remove it.

BITE.clue: Mammalian wound that needs amoxicillin-clavulanate because skin organisms and mouth flora are both involved
BITE.rationale: Cat and human bites become infected often. Hand bites are referred; do not close an infected bite primarily; update tetanus status; rabies prophylaxis depends on the animal and the local health guidance, not on a guess.

LICE.clue: Head infestation treated with a pediculicide and a repeat treatment timed to the life cycle; exclude from school only until treatment starts
LICE.rationale: Permethrin or ivermectin lotion is used, and nits are combed. Failure may be resistance, not poor parenting; lindane is avoided; bedding is washed, but fumigating the house is unnecessary; body lice, unlike head lice, are associated with typhus in people living unsheltered.

PINWORM.clue: Nocturnal perianal itch in a child; the morning tape test finds eggs, and the household is treated
PINWORM.rationale: Enterobius is not found well on a random stool ova-and-parasite exam. Pyrantel or albendazole treats it, and bedding is washed; reinfection is common; it does not cause diarrhea as its main feature.

PYRANTEL.clue: Over-the-counter anthelmintic used for pinworm, with a repeat dose to catch newly hatched worms
PYRANTEL.rationale: Pyrantel pamoate is given once and often repeated in two weeks. Treat household contacts; it is not the drug for all intestinal parasites; handwashing after toileting and before food interrupts the fecal-oral cycle.

ENTEROBIUS.clue: Pinworm genus that lays eggs on the perianal skin at night
ENTEROBIUS.rationale: Enterobius vermicularis causes itch, not malabsorption. The tape test is done in the morning before bathing; all close contacts are treated; vaginal itch in a girl can be from migration of the worms.

ROSEOLA.clue: High fever in an infant that breaks as a rash appears, caused by human herpesvirus 6
ROSEOLA.rationale: Roseola is also called exanthem subitum. The child looks better when the rash arrives; febrile seizures can occur during the fever; it is not measles, which has cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and Koplik spots while the person is still ill.

RUBEOLA.clue: Measles, with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a rash that starts at the head
RUBEOLA.rationale: Measles is airborne and is reported. Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa precede the rash; vitamin A is used in children under current guidance; two vaccine doses prevent it; a febrile rash in an unvaccinated person after exposure is measles until proven otherwise.

KOPLIK.clue: White spots on the buccal mucosa that appear before the measles rash
KOPLIK.rationale: Koplik spots are a pathognomonic early finding of measles. They are easy to miss if you do not look in the mouth; once the cephalocaudal rash is florid, the spots may already have faded; isolate the person and report the case.

MUMPS.clue: Viral parotitis prevented by the childhood combined live vaccine; testicular inflammation is a complication
MUMPS.rationale: Mumps swells the parotid and can be unilateral. Orchitis threatens fertility in adolescents and adults; it is reported and is contagious before the swelling; vaccination has made it uncommon but outbreaks still occur in close quarters.

PAROTID.clue: Salivary gland that swells in mumps and that can also swell from a stone or bacterial infection
PAROTID.rationale: Mumps is bilateral or unilateral viral parotitis with fever and no pus at the duct. Bacterial parotitis is unilateral, toxic, and pus can be expressed at Stensen duct, more often in dehydrated older adults; a stone causes mealtime swelling.

PARVOVIRUS.clue: Cause of fifth disease, a slapped-cheek rash that is dangerous in pregnancy and in sickle cell disease
PARVOVIRUS.rationale: Parvovirus B19 is usually no longer contagious once the rash appears. In pregnancy it can cause fetal anemia and hydrops; in sickle cell disease it causes aplastic crisis; adults more often have joint pain than a slapped cheek.

ENTEROVIRUS.clue: Virus family that causes painful mouth lesions and a rash on the hands and feet; the main risk is dehydration
ENTEROVIRUS.rationale: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is supportive care. Watch infants who will not drink; nail shedding can follow weeks later; it is not the same as measles or Kawasaki disease; herpangina is the related painful posterior-mouth form.

MASTITIS.clue: Breast inflammation in a nursing parent; keep removing milk, and add an antibiotic when infection is likely
MASTITIS.rationale: Inflammatory mastitis is often managed with continued emptying, rest, and anti-inflammatory care. Antibiotics are added when infection is likely, an abscess needs drainage, and a breast that is not improving is re-examined rather than given endless antibiotics.

EDINBURGH.clue: Ten-item questionnaire used to screen for depression in pregnancy and after birth
EDINBURGH.rationale: A positive screen is not a diagnosis. It finds postpartum depression the person may not volunteer, and any thought of self-harm needs same-day assessment rather than a routine follow-up.

COLOSTRUM.clue: First milk, rich in antibodies and produced in small amounts before mature milk comes in
COLOSTRUM.rationale: Colostrum is enough for a healthy newborn's early feeds. Frequent nursing brings in mature milk; supplementation is not routine; a newborn who is not feeding, is jaundiced early, or is losing too much weight needs a feeding evaluation.

VISION.clue: Yellow-tinged sight with nausea and an irregular pulse suggests toxicity from a narrow-index heart medicine
VISION.rationale: Digoxin toxicity is more likely when potassium or magnesium is low or kidney function falls. The drug is not first-line disease-modifying therapy for heart failure, though it can reduce hospitalizations; the antidote is digoxin-specific antibody.

ULTRASOUND.clue: Sound-wave imaging that confirms a deep-vein clot, a gallbladder problem, or a first-trimester pregnancy location
ULTRASOUND.rationale: Duplex ultrasound is the usual first study for a suspected leg clot. Pelvic ultrasound looks for an intrauterine pregnancy when ectopic pregnancy is possible; it does not replace a pregnancy test or a clinical decision to send an unstable person to emergency care.
